articles.title: Spain grows fruit and vegetables for Europe — but it's running out of water
articles.summary: Spain's southern coast produces up to 25% of Europe's fruit and vegetables. But amid intensive farming, climate change and illegal wells, the water it takes to grow them is drying up.

image.caption: Spain's southern coast grows one-quarter of Europe's fruit and vegetablesImage: Bernat Armangue/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Donana National Park in southwestern Spain — one of Europe's most important wetlands, home to millions of migratory birds and threatened species like the Iberian lynx — is running dry. But rising temperatures and drought caused by climate change are only part of the problem.

The UNESCO-protected region on the Atlantic coast relies on an underground aquifer that's been tapped by hundreds of illegal wells. The reason: Europe's fruit and vegetable supply. Spain provides one-quarter of Europe's fresh produce, supplying colder parts of the continent with fruit and vegetables year-round.

The scale of water extraction in Spain is staggering: In 2016, WWF Spain estimated that the Donana wetland was home to over 1,000 illegal wells and more than 1,700 ponds illegally irrigating an area as big as 4,200 football fields.

blocks.caption: The 'sea of plastic' in Almeria is a massive expanse of plastic-covered greenhouses key to Spain's agricultural productionImage: Viajar24h/Pond5 Images/IMAGO

blocks.text: "It's gotten hotter every year. And the water dries up so quickly," one local resident in the town of El Rocio, just north of the wetlands, told DW.

"For me, day to day, the main issue is my animals," said another, hitching his horse up to a tourist carriage. "I have to draw water for them, but the well doesn't have enough water to provide it all at once."
Strawberries are lucrative — but come with a cost

The Donana area used to be royal hunting grounds, consisting of marshes and ponds. In the early 20th century, parts began to be used for dryland farming, agriculture in arid regions that relies heavily on rainwater.

But in 1971, Spain — still under the dictatorship of General Francisco Franco — declared the region's irrigation to be of national interest. The Almonte-Marismas Plan, named after the aquifer it tapped into, was part of a massive, state-sponsored effort to increase food production.

Authorities decided to bet on strawberries, which they called "red gold." According to calculations based on FAO data, strawberries can yield up to €150,000 (about $170,000) in gross revenue per hectare per year, compared to roughly €20,000 for potatoes or €15,000 for grapes.

But growing strawberries at scale also meant using a lot more water. Authorities handed out generous quotas and allotments, seemingly without considering how much extraction the aquifer could handle. Even those legal quotas weren't enough for the ever-expanding fields.

blocks.caption: Strawberries are one of Spain's most lucrative crops, earning up to €150,000 in gross revenue per hectare per yearImage: Adri Salido/Anadolu Agency/picture alliance

blocks.text: Farmers turned to illegal wells and reservoirs to make up the difference. They built them to stockpile water, draining supplies from local residents and the UNESCO World Heritage Site next door.

"There was extreme drought and lack of attention from the administration," said Pedro Banez, of the Condado Water Users' Association. "And we found ourselves with a number of farms — or parts of farms — that fell outside the land classified as irrigable agricultural land."
Police, NGOs track down water thieves

The turning point came in 2019 when, following numerous reports of unlawful wells, a 2-year-old fell into deep, reportedly illegal borehole on farmland near Malaga and died. In the aftermath, Spain's Civil Guard police force created dedicated units focused on water theft.
Two years after that, in 2021, the Court of Justice of the European Union ruled that Spain had failed to protect the Donana aquifer, finding the country in violation of EU law.

Today, police and NGOs like WWF Spain track illegal extraction — near Donana, and other overtaxed agricultural regions across the country — using a mix of old and new tools. They start with satellite images of the region, comparing them against land rights maps to flag areas that appear greener than their legal status allows. Drones follow, giving investigators a closer look at where the water is actually coming from.
With Spain in drought, farmers drill illegal wells
Some wells are completely illegal. Others are legal but extract more than they're allowed, which requires closer, on-site inspection to prove.

Investigators check the flow meters that measure how much water a well is pulling. Tampering is common, often using a powerful magnet which disrupts the internal mechanism of the flow meter, allowing water to pass through unrecorded.
Farmers caught extracting illegally can be charged with crimes against the environment and fraud. Most face fines, but sentences can run up to five years in prison.
Spain's government, farmers tackle water misuse

In a bid to undo decades of overuse, local and national authorities have negotiated a €1.4 billion joint plan. The government has continued shutting down illegal wells, sealing almost 300 in the Donana region alone.
Officials have also started buying up farmland, rewilding it and turning it into protected areas, while setting up funds to create jobs in other sectors like tourism and renewable energy.
Spain's invisible war for water
Farmers, meanwhile, have had to change how they water their crops.

Many have switched to drip irrigation systems, where each plant gets its own individual dripper, paired with moisture sensors that report exactly how much water a plant needs. That cuts down on the overuse of both water and fertilizer.
Farmers have also begun planting less water-intensive crops and shifting their growing season to colder months.
Sustainable solutions to secure water
Spain isn't alone in confronting this problem. As economies mature, fruit and vegetable production starts being outsourced to places with cheaper labor, fewer restrictions and more sun.

Mexico, Brazil and Colombia grow food for parts of the US, while countries in southeast Asia export a lot of produce to China or Japan. Some countries in northern Africa, including Morocco and Egypt, also supply fresh fruits and vegetables to their European neighbors to the north. But, as in Spain, intensive agriculture has strained local water supplies.
Saving Europe's largest wetlands

Morocco has tried to turn the tide by using satellite comparisons to monitor irrigation and offering subsidies for farmers who switch to drip irrigation. In India, the government is trying to move farmers toward less water-intensive crops.
And in California, the US state has paid farmers to halt certain types of irrigation and introduced legislation to monitor and allocate water more sustainably.

Securing water, no longer seen as an unlimited resource, will increasingly be a challenge as the effects of climate change intensify. Addressing overextraction will take a coordinated effort from governments, farmers and the industries that depend on their water.
Additional research by Nicole Ris. Edited by: Martin Kuebler, Sarah Steffen

articles.title: Baste Duterte says Sara didn’t ask to favor Gencorp, intervene in procurement
articles.summary: The Davao City mayor also denies having personal knowledge of his sister's business interests

blocks.text: WITNESS. Davao City Mayor Sebastian 'Baste' Duterte takes the witness stand on Day 31 of the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte on September 29, 2026.
Senate Social Media Unit
The Davao City mayor also denies having personal knowledge of his sister's business interests

MANILA, Philippines – Davao City Mayor Sebastian “Baste” Duterte testified before the impeachment court on Tuesday, September 29, that Vice President Sara Duterte noted did not interfere in his city government’s procurement process, more so asked him to favor Gencorp Industries, Inc. in deals.

Responding to questions from his older sister’s defense team, Baste denied that the Vice President directly or indirectly intervened or participated in any procurement of the Davao City local government unit.
“So you confirm that there is also no request for favor, particularly for Gencorp Industries, Inc.?” defense deputy spokesperson and counsel Justin Nichol Gular asked the mayor.
“No,” Baste replied.

“No particular request for accommodation, particularly for GenCorp Industries, Inc.? No request or special treatment for GenCorp Industries, Inc.?” Gular added. “None,” the Davao City mayor said in response.

For his last question during the cross-examination, Gular asked Baste that as the brother of the Vice President who has known her for years, did he think that it’s in her character seek special favors in relation to government procurement deals?

blocks.caption: Baste Duterte says Sara didn’t ask to favor Gencorp, intervene in procurement

blocks.text: Counsel for the prosecution Theodore Te objected, saying that Gular’s question calls for a conclusion and violates the character and opinion rule. However, presiding officer Chiz Escudero overruled the objection and allowed Gular’s final question.

“Now, being the brother of the Vice President herself, having known her for years, do you think that it is in her character as a person and as a politician to request for any favor, accommodation, or special treatment in relation to government contracts of a corporation?” the defense lawyer asked, repeating his question.
“No,” said Baste.

The prosecution is in the middle of presenting its evidence on the Vice President’s alleged unexplained wealth — the third article of impeachment against her. The prosecution is scrutinizing Gencorp because it is allegedly linked to Duterte.

A Rappler investigation revealed that Gencorp cornered P15 million in food and catering contracts from Davao City Hall and PhilHealth between 2022 and 2025 — the years when Baste is sitting as mayor. The Dutertes — from Rodrigo to Baste — have been ruling Davao City for almost 40 years. (READ: Sara Duterte’s company won millions’ worth of contracts from Davao City Hall)

The prosecution presented Baste as a hostile witness on Tuesday to show alleged conflict of interest in these deals. This is because Baste is sitting as mayor and head of the procurement agency, and yet Gencorp was able to corner contracts from the city hall.

During the cross, Baste also denied having personal knowledge of his sister’s business interests, and of any information where she has stock holdings or investments in, as well corporations she has beneficial ownership of.
The Davao City mayor also claimed that he did not have personal knowledge of his sister’s disclosure in her Statement of Assets, Liabilities, and Net Worth (SALN).

blocks.caption: Baste Duterte says Sara didn’t ask to favor Gencorp, intervene in procurement

blocks.text: “And for the record, why don’t you have personal knowledge on these matters despite being the brother of the vice president?” Gular asked.
“We simply do not discuss this. And I did not ask. It’s her privacy,” Baste responded.
“And again, for the record, why don’t you have any personal knowledge on this?” Gular again told Baste when he asked about the SALN question.
“It’s not my responsibility to know this,” Baste replied. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Trillanes questions Baste Duterte's remarks over VP Sara's business interests
articles.summary: Former senator Antonio Trillanes IV on Tuesday questioned the statements made by Davao City Mayor Sebastian "Baste" Duterte over the business interests of his sister, Vice President Sara Duterte.

blocks.text: Published September 29, 2026 5:49pm
Former senator Antonio Trillanes IV on Tuesday questioned the statements made by Davao City Mayor Sebastian "Baste" Duterte over the business interests of his sister, Vice President Sara Duterte.

Trillanes said all mayors in the Philippines could enter into contracts with their siblings and simply "feign ignorance" after the mayor's remarks during the Day 31 of the impeachment trial of his sister.

"Kung pwede ‘yung sinasabi niya, lahat ng mayor sa Pilipinas, pwede makipag-kontrata sa kapatid sa kanila. They will just feign ignorance. So think about that. Ayun ang implication dito," the former senator told reporters.
(If what he's saying is allowed, then all mayors in the Philippines could enter into contracts with their siblings. They will just feign ignorance. So think about that. That's the implication here.)
The mayor appeared before the impeachment court to testify about his sister's alleged link to GenCorp Industries, a company stated in her Statement of Assets, Liabilities, and Net Worth (SALN).
But Baste maintained that he has no personal knowledge about his sister's business interests.
"We do not discuss it," the younger Duterte said when asked by House private prosecutor Theodore Te.
Sara Duterte declared GenCorp. Industries Inc. as one of her business interests in her 2024 and 2025 Statement of Assets, Liabilities and Net Worth (SALN).
The Vice President’s name, however, is not reflected as one of the shareholders of GenCorp. Industries Inc. in the company’s records submitted to the Securities and Exchange Commission.

When asked how he felt seeing the Davao mayor in person, Trillanes, a staunch critic of the Dutertes, said: "Nakita natin, at least finally up close nakita ko. Sana nakita rin ng kababayan natin yung nakita ko. Whatever that is, saka na lang natin i-elaborate."
(I saw [him]—at least I finally saw him up close. I hope the public also saw what I saw. Whatever that is, I'll just elaborate on it later.)
Moreover, Trillanes said that he is hoping to testify on Wednesday in relation to funds and bank accounts as the impeachment court tackles the Vice President's alleged unexplained wealth.
However, the impeachment court has yet to issue a subpoena to Trillanes.
"I hope to testify tomorrow. So abangan na lang natin ‘yun," he said.
(I hope to testify tomorrow. So let's just stay tuned for that.) —RF, GMA News

articles.title: Trial of live facial recognition cameras in London stations ends with one false positive
articles.summary:
Freedom of information request shows six-month trial cost £320,000, used almost 100 police hours and resulted in no arrests

A six-month trial of live facial recognition (LFR) technology in…

blocks.text: A six-month trial of live facial recognition (LFR) technology in London’s railway stations that cost more than £320,000 and almost 100 hours of police officers’ time ended in one false match against a watchlist of suspects and no arrests.

More than half a million faces were scanned between February and July this year in some of the capital’s busiest transport hubs during the British Transport Police (BTP) trial of the surveillance technology, which aimed to help catch offenders and people breaching court orders.

A freedom of information document obtained by Liberty Investigates and shared with the Guardian shows that equipment hire and police staffing for the 18 deployments across the trial cost the taxpayer £320,786 and led to only one alert on a watchlist, which turned out to be an incorrect identification, also known as a false positive.
Last month BTP announced it was extending the trial for a further four months and expanding the deployments to include London Underground stations.

When Transport for London announced its support for the extension of the trial, it said LFR technology “will target and identify people on police watchlists at key stations chosen for maximum impact” and would “specifically tackle violence against women and girls, whose travel behaviours are shaped by experiences of sexual harassment and sexual offences”.

Fraser Sampson, the former biometrics and surveillance camera commissioner for the UK, said the police needed to show that the use of the technology was proportionate. “There many variables and all need to align: the choice of location, times of day, make up of the watchlist and likelihood of people being present and many more.”

Sampson, who is now a non-executive director of Facewatch, a company that operates facial recognition systems in shops, added: “We know the technology works but using it in supermarkets to deter shoplifters and prevent attacks on staff is very different from deploying it to catch people on a public transport network.
“Success in a shop means no such people coming in. Success for the police trying to catch people means people being caught. In that respect the trial doesn’t appear to have been very fruitful.
“Everything depends on the police watchlists; if you’re not on a watchlist, the live FRT cameras do not ‘see’ you and they don’t retain your image in the same way as CCTV cameras.

“However, they are processing special category personal data and the technology must be used in a way that is appropriate, proportionate and necessary. It’s for the police to show how any deployment meets those criteria and – as the ICO [information commissioner’s office] has recently reported – for their oversight boards to hold them firmly to account in doing so.”
More than half of police forces in England and Wales have now deployed LFR on British streets, according to an analysis by Liberty Investigates.

The Metropolitan police and London mayor’s office announced this summer that it was planning to install fixed LFR cameras in the capital’s West End. Sadiq Khan the mayor of London, has since confirmed it will be used on the newly pedestrianised Oxford Street.

A recent report from parliament’s joint committee on human rights, which called on the government to introduce a law to address the threat of artificial intelligence to human rights, identified the rollout of live facial recognition technology as a “particularly clear example of risk”.

Bell Ribeiro-Addy, Labour MP for Clapham and Brixton Hill, said: “Live facial recognition technologies are a serious invasion of our privacy. The government should be suspending their rollout until there are stronger safeguards in place, including a proper legal framework.”

A BTP spokesperson said it had launched the LFR pilot to “to understand how the technology could most effectively support the identification of wanted offenders and individuals who may pose a risk to passengers and staff”.

They added: “During these deployments, officers have made a number of associated arrests, including for assault, theft, possession of an offensive weapon, breach of a criminal behaviour order and public order offences, as well as locating individuals wanted by the courts and other police forces. As these arrests did not result directly from an LFR alert, they are not included within LFR performance data.

“Throughout the pilot, we have continued to refine how the capability is deployed within the railway environment. This has included developments to deployment locations, operating procedures, equipment and watchlist construction.

“A particularly important point is that watchlist growth has been deliberate, controlled and aligned to BTP policy. We began with a more limited watchlist whilst ensuring data quality, governance and safeguarding arrangements were robust.”

articles.title: Dale Vince plans London-wide news operation to take on ‘rightwing bias’ in the media
articles.summary:
Green energy entrepreneur plans rescue package for the group behind the Camden New Journal, Islington Tribune and Westminster Extra

The green energy entrepreneur and Labour donor Dale Vince…

blocks.text: The green energy entrepreneur and Labour donor Dale Vince is planning to launch a London-wide news operation, as part of a “rescue” of one of the capital’s most highly regarded local newspapers.

Vince, who has vowed to take on what he sees as rightwing bias in the UK media, said he would invest “whatever it takes” to support the loss-making group behind the Camden New Journal (CNJ), Islington Tribune and Westminster Extra.

He told the Guardian he was already looking at expanding the Westminster edition to cover London-wide issues, in an attempt to serve a city in which a series of major newsrooms have closed or drastically shrunk over the past 20 years.

“We’re going to go forward together to put the CNJ on a better financial footing and take it digital – properly digital,” he said. “At the same time, [we will] get behind the Westminster edition and make that an edition for the wider London area.
“I think London is missing a local paper now, with the demise of a couple that have gone before. It’s quite a bold plan, that we might morph the Westminster edition.
“We might call it the north, south, east and Westminster edition, in a kind of nod to our intended larger audience.”

Vince’s rescue package for the titles, which has not been formally finalised, is one of several attempts being made to revitalise local journalism in London. Despite its 9m population, media outlets have struggled to support large London-focused newsrooms.

The Evening Standard, which has been published for almost 200 years, shut down its daily newspaper in 2024. It was replaced with a weekly edition renamed the London Standard, with a greater focus on arts and culture.

Other attempts to run daily freesheets failed. The London Paper, launched by Rupert Murdoch’s News International, now News UK, closed in 2009 after just three years. Its rival, London Lite, published by the owner of the Daily Mail, closed later that year.
Meanwhile, Metro, a national freesheet distributed in UK cities including London, is undergoing major structural changes to put it on a “sustainable footing”.
However, journalism focused on London has been boosted in recent years by the arrival of small, subscription-based operations.

Jim Waterson, a former Guardian journalist who founded the London Centric news site that now has more than 5,000 paying subscribers, said Vince had chosen to help a local group that had resisted “the disastrous choice in the 2010s to abandon quality for chasing clicks at all costs”.
However, he said the success of his own “back-to-basics local journalism” outlet was still “only enough money to support a tiny operation that’s still run from a kitchen table”.

“Vince has also realised that London is also one of the UK’s worst local news deserts,” Waterson said. “The challenge that we all face is how to get the funding to grow our audience without becoming financially unsustainable.”
While not large, the Camden New Journal group still employs 18 people, according to recent financial records. It spent a chunk of its cash reserves in the last year.
Vince said he was not supporting the Camden New Journal and its related titles “for business reasons”.
“I’m motivated by the impact of local journalism,” he said. “I’m motivated by the bias of media in our country more broadly – the rightwing bias – and trying to do something about that.”
Vince has already launched an online publication, Babelfish. He said he would consider writing comment pieces for the London titles, but would generally be a “hands-off” investor.

“Big picture-wise, I’ve got a view of the world and how things should be, and the Camden people already fit within that,” he said. “There’s no kind of culture clash and I write op-eds for all kinds of people already. I would absolutely write op-eds for the Camden [New Journal], but it wouldn’t be a requirement.”

articles.title: Sydney teen taken to hospital after falling from moving bus on northern beaches
articles.summary:
Transport for NSW, bus operator and Rail, Tram and Bus union investigate after incident on Monday evening

  • Get our

blocks.text: Investigations are under way after a teenage girl fell from a moving double-decker bus on to a busy road in Sydney’s northern beaches.
Emergency services were called to Manly Road at Seaforth on Monday evening after the teenager fell from the B-Line bus near the Spit Bridge.
She was treated at the scene for head and hip injuries and taken to Royal North Shore hospital, where a spokesperson confirmed on Tuesday she remained in a stable condition.

A Transport for NSW spokesperson said it was aware of the incident on Spit Road and that the bus had been withdrawn from service while an investigation by bus operator Keolis Northern Beaches and the department takes place.
“The passenger was treated at the scene and taken to hospital with minor injuries,” they said. “We wish the passenger all the best in her recovery.”
The incident has also been reported to the Office of Transport Safety Investigations.

On Tuesday, the Rail, Tram and Bus Union (RTBU) said Keolis Northern Beaches, “must urgently explain how a door on one of its B-Line buses reportedly failed” and that it was investigating reports from drivers that doors on the fleet had opened unexpectedly in the past.
RTBU NSW Tram and Bus Division secretary Peter Grech said private operator Keolis and Transport for NSW must “come clean” about whether warnings had been ignored.

“A 16-year-old girl fell out of a moving bus … on to one of the Northern Beaches’ busiest roads. It is horrifying to think how much worse this could have been,” Grech said. “She should have been safe on that bus and this was undoubtedly a highly traumatic experience for her.

“Drivers are telling us this may not be the first time one of these doors has opened unexpectedly. We are currently checking the circumstances, but Keolis cannot leave passengers wondering whether there were warnings it simply failed to act on.
“If a door can open while a bus is moving, then that bus cannot be carrying the public,” he said.
after newsletter promotion

Keolis responded to Guardian Australia’s request for comment on Tuesday afternoon with a statement confirming it was “aware of an incident that occurred last night on our B-Line service which resulted in a passenger falling from the bus near the Spit Bridge at Seaforth”.
“Our immediate thoughts are with the passenger and her family and wishing for a swift recovery.”
It is understood Bustech double-decker B-Line buses have been taken out of service, although Keolis and Transport for NSW have not confirmed which vehicles were withdrawn or when.
It has not been established when and how earlier concerns were reported to Keolis management, the response drivers received or what steps were taken to control the risk.
It is understood the union is seeking records from Keolis and Transport for NSW under the work health and safety act as part of its investigation.

articles.title: Former snooker world champion Graeme Dott jailed for child sexual abuse
articles.summary:
Dott, 49, receives seven-year sentence after abusing a boy and a girl in what judge says was ‘gross violation of trust’

The former snooker world champion Graeme Dott has been jailed for…

blocks.text: The former snooker world champion Graeme Dott has been jailed for seven years at the high court in Edinburgh after being convicted of sexually abusing two children.

In August, Dott was found guilty of sexually abusing a boy and a girl after a five-day trial at Glasgow high court. The court heard that the 2006 world champion inappropriately touched and exposed himself to both children. He denied the charges but was convicted of two counts of lewd, indecent and libidinous behaviour by a majority verdict.
Dott appeared at the high court in Edinburgh on Tuesday, where the judge, Lord Harrower, told him he had “robbed the complainers of a significant part of their childhood”.
Imposing a backdated sentence of seven years, he said the 49-year-old’s behaviour had involved a “gross violation of trust”.

Between 1993 and 1996, Dott targeted a girl on multiple occasions. The woman, now in her 40s, told the trial that the abuse began when he started “caressing” her bottom over her clothing while giving her a piggyback.

She told the court that Dott had told her not to tell anyone that he was sexually abusing her, describing incidents when he had suggested playing a “guessing game”. He would expose himself to her, she said, and began touching her with different parts of his body, including his penis.

The second victim, a man now in his late 20s, was targeted between 2006 and 2010. He said he was sexually abused by Dott on multiple occasions, with the snooker player touching him inappropriately, kissing him and performing sexual acts. He told the court a lot of the abuse took place while he was in a shower, when Dott would come in either partly or completely undressed.
“He would … come into the shower and put soap on my body and wash me in the shower,” the man told the court. “While he was washing me he would touch me in inappropriate places.”

He said looking back at it now, Dott was “clearly getting sexual gratification from it”, and he was “pleasuring himself” while this was taking place. The man said that because of his age at the time, he “did not know what was going on”, and it was only later he realised the interaction “wasn’t right”. The witness also described abuse which took place in a car, where he said Dott would kiss him on the face, head and lips and “push himself up against me”.
Harrower remanded Dott in custody and his name was added to the sex offender register.

Dott, who turned professional in 1994, won the World Snooker Championship in 2006, defeating Peter Ebdon in the final at the Crucible in Sheffield. He reached the final in two other years but was beaten by Ronnie O’Sullivan in 2004 and Neil Robertson in 2010.
Following his conviction, Dott’s name was removed from World Snooker’s hall of fame.

articles.title: Impeachment court admonishes prosecutor Tolosa over public statements
articles.summary: The Senate impeachment court has admonished private prosecutor Benjamin Tolosa Jr. over his previous public comments on the impeachment case against Vice President Sara Duterte.

blocks.text: Published September 29, 2026 5:36pm
The Senate impeachment court has admonished private prosecutor Benjamin Tolosa Jr. over his previous public comments on the impeachment case against Vice President Sara Duterte.
Tolosa confirmed this on Tuesday, saying the court urged him to exercise greater restraint in speaking about the impeachment case, although it did not impose a fine on him.

“I’ve received the order of the court and based on my reading, there’s no express finding there that I violated Rule 18 [prohibiting discussion on the merits of the case]," Tolosa said in a press conference.
"I will assume that the reason for this is that the court listened and considered the explanation that we gave in our answer,” he added.
Tolosa said the court order did not address his defense that his statements were protected under the doctrine allowing fair, true and accurate reporting of court proceedings.
“There’s also no statement there that contradicts my other defense that they [the topics I spoke about] are procedural matters that are outside the scope of Rule 18,” Tolosa said.

“Nonetheless, even if there’s no express statement that I violated the rule, there’s at the end an admonition to exercise greater restraint in giving public statements that may affect the merits of the case,” he added.

The sub judice rule is provided under Article 18 of the Rules on Impeachment. It states that the presiding officer and members of the Senate “shall refrain from making any comments and disclosures in public pertaining to the merits of a pending impeachment trial.”
The rule also states that “the same [prohibition] shall likewise apply to the prosecutors, the person impeached, and their respective counsel and witnesses.”

One of the statements cited by the court involved Tolosa’s summary of an argument raised by his fellow private prosecutor Mae Divinagracia. The argument concerned the defense’s claim that the unusual names of confidential fund recipients were aliases, which the defense raised only after three weeks of the impeachment trial.
The prosecution had pointed out that the defense did not identify the names as aliases in its verified answer to the impeachment complaint.

Another statement cited by the court involved Tolosa’s remark that the prosecution would not present additional evidence that would merely be cumulative, particularly if the prosecutors believed they had already presented sufficient evidence.
Tolosa said he respectfully disagreed with the court’s admonition but recognized its authority.

“With all due respect, I respectfully disagree with respect to that admonition because, as I’ve stated, there is no finding that I violated the rule. While I respectfully disagree, of course, I respect the authority of the impeachment court as an institution,” he said.
Tolosa said he would comply with the court’s admonition and avoid allowing the issue to distract from the ongoing impeachment proceedings.

“I will not belabor the point and I will, of course, respect that admonition and hence be even more careful in giving statements moving forward. I just don’t want this matter to cause any distraction since our focus should really be on what’s important that we’re currently hearing,” he added.
Tolosa earlier maintained that his challenged statements did not fall under the prohibition in Rule 18 because they concerned procedural matters and did not evaluate the merits of the case.

“The others merely recounted matters already placed on the public record during the proceedings, fairly and accurately, in good faith, and without editorial comment. Accordingly, there is no basis for citing the undersigned counsel for violation of Rule 18,” Tolosa said in his answer.

Tolosa maintained that his statements, when viewed in context, did not assess disputed facts, witness credibility, evidence, the validity of the impeachment charges or defenses, or how the case should be decided.— MCG, GMA News

articles.title: New UK homes in flood-risk areas could become uninsurable, says Aviva boss
articles.summary: Amanda Blanc says flooding threat is ‘absolutely increasing’, as she also warns ministers over ‘kite flying’ before budget

blocks.text: The boss of Britain’s biggest insurer has warned that homes being built now could become uninsurable in the future because they are sited in flood-risk areas.

Amanda Blanc, the chief executive of Aviva, said the flooding threat was “absolutely increasing”. Assuming current construction patterns continue, 115,000 homes will be built in flood zones in the next decade.
“That doesn’t seem to me to make sense. We need to think about where those homes are being built,” she told the BBC.

About 6.3m homes and businesses in England are at risk of flooding, according to the Environment Agency. This could increase to around 8m, or one in four properties, by mid-century as the climate crisis worsens, it warned in August.
Blanc told the BBC’s Big Boss Interview podcast that England was “for sure” building properties that might become uninsurable in the future.
“It’s very well known where these flooding areas are. Let’s think very carefully about homes that are being built.”
She said a lot could be done to mitigate damage, adding: “You can do all sorts of different things to your property to make it more or less vulnerable to flood.”
According to Aviva’s research, nearly a third of new homes built in 2024 will be at risk of some flooding by 2050, and one in seven will be at medium-to-high risk of flooding.
After the very wet and stormy winter in the UK in 2023-24, the Met Office estimated that such winters had gone from once in 80-year events to once in 20-year events.
Blanc also called on the government to avoid policy “kite flying” before John Healey’s first budget as chancellor on 28 October.
after newsletter promotion
Aviva is a leading private pension provider, and speculation about changes to pensions led to a jump in withdrawals in the run-up to the budget in the last two years.

“Effectively we saw in the last year 30 times the normal withdrawal from pensions that we would normally see, which is clearly something which customers may regret afterwards because once you take your tax-free lump sum out, you can’t put it back in,” she said.
“So we would say be very, very thoughtful about the things that you are testing, thinking about.”

articles.title: Danger zone: why war in the Middle East has landed the RBA’s inflation fight in tricky territory
articles.summary:
The Reserve Bank appears ready to push harder against inflation but it comes with a greater risk for the economy

The fight against inflation has entered a new, more dangerous…

blocks.text: The fight against inflation has entered a new, more dangerous phase.
For years, the Reserve Bank has been attempting, as gently as possible, to steer inflation back to its 2.5% target while trying to retain as many of the post-pandemic job gains as possible.
“That still remains the strategy,” Michele Bullock, the RBA’s governor, told journalists on Tuesday afternoon, an hour after the board announced the fourth interest rate hike for the year.
Unemployment has climbed by 1 percentage point over the past four years, sure, but at 4.6% it’s “still quite low historically,” Bullock said.
Other central banks have managed to get inflation lower, sure, but at the cost of higher unemployment, she said.
Yet there are signs that the central bank may be losing faith in this “slowly, slowly” strategy.
Bullock explained the RBA has been outside the 2-3% target range for six years now. That’s a problem, because households and businesses need to believe that inflation will fall again, one day.
“We came in [to the range] briefly in 2025, and then we’ve popped back out again. We are aiming to get it back,” she said.
But how to get inflation back under control “in a reasonable time”, when unreasonable things keep happening?
It’s the unending Middle East conflict that now looms as the biggest threat to the RBA’s careful approach to taming inflation.
As Bullock said: “When the Middle East conflict first started, everyone was sort of thinking, ‘Oh, it will probably not last very long’.”
“Well, that’s clearly not true. It’s lasted, and there doesn’t seem to be any end to it,” she said.
Fuel prices, fertiliser prices, transport prices are now all “permanently higher”.
“So this idea that they would go up and then come down again just hasn’t happened.”
after newsletter promotion

The RBA governor is worried that businesses are also coming to the same conclusion, and will start lifting their prices. That will make it even harder to get inflation back to target without a more dramatic increase in interest rates.
Bullock and her board have long made it clear they will “do what it takes” to get inflation back to target, a phrase they repeated on Tuesday.

After Tuesday’s announcement, a number of economists are betting the RBA will hike again in six weeks’ time, at the Melbourne Cup day meeting. Financial markets see a 50% chance of yet another increase next year.
All up, it sounds like the RBA is ready to start pushing harder against inflation.
That might be the right call, but it increases the risk the central bank will push too hard and, in Bullock’s words, drive the economy into a “dramatic slowdown”.
“Hopefully, in the next couple of years, when we get inflation back down, this will have all been worth it.”

articles.title: Lord Allan Velasco out of Philippines, BI confirms
articles.summary: No hold departure order or derogatory record prevented the ex-speaker's exit.

blocks.text: September 29, 2026 | 5:09pm

Image shows dismissed police officer Rodulfo Gracioso Jr. (center) with former speaker Lord Allan Velasco and Vice President Sara Duterte. This is one of the photographs included with the affidavit Gracioso submitted to the NBI.
STAR / File
MANILA, Philippines — Fformer House Speaker Lord Allan Velasco has not returned from abroad with yet no cases filed against him, the Bureau of Immigration (BI) confirmed on Tuesday, September 29.
Velasco is among the subjects of the National Bureau of Investigation's probe looking into the allegations of Velasco's former security aide, Rodulfo Gracioso Jr.
The former Marinduque representative has not been issued a hold departure order or other derogatory record that would have prevented him from leaving the country,
Velasco cleared immigration controls without any legal impediment to his departure, the immigration bureau said, citing travel records. It, however, refused to bare more details.
"The BI cannot disclose further details concerning an individual's immigration records due to data privacy concerns," the bureau said.
A hold departure order is a court-issued directive that prevents a person covered by the order from leaving the Philippines while the restriction remains in effect.
"The Bureau remains committed to the consistent enforcement of immigration laws and policies while ensuring the proper protection and confidentiality of personal information," it added.

NBI Director Melvin Matibag separately said Tuesday that Velasco left the country on August 30 and had yet to return. Matibag said immigration records initially showed that Velasco was expected to return on September 14.

His departure therefore preceded the public emergence in late September of allegations by Gracioso, a dismissed police officer, involving purported cash deliveries to Vice President Sara Duterte he made for Velasco .
NBI looking into cash delivery claims

The confirmation of Velasco's whereabouts comes as the NBI investigates allegations contained in Gracioso's sworn affidavit. The bureau has said it plans to invite Velasco and other individuals named in the affidavit to hear their side.
The Philippine National Police said Gracioso had been detailed as a security officer or staff member of Velasco, although it did not immediately specify the period of his assignment.

Gracioso alleged that, on Velasco's instructions, he delivered suitcases containing cash to Duterte, former President Rodrigo Duterte and Davao City Rep. Paolo "Pulong" Duterte. He claimed he made more than 20 deliveries to the vice president totaling more than P2 billion and also alleged delivering more than P1 billion to the former president.
The allegations are being investigated by the NBI.
Velasco's camp has denied Gracioso's allegations, describing them as fabricated and inconsistent with verifiable events. Duterte has likewise denied knowing Gracioso or receiving money from him.

articles.title: Death of Tenessee sheriff’s office canine leads to criminal investigation
articles.summary:
Patrol dog’s handler resigned after it emerged Bart had died of heatstroke due to severe dehydration in nearly 101F heat

The recent death of a

blocks.text: The recent death of a Tennessee sheriff’s office dog after being left in an outdoor kennel without water for a day and a half in excessive heat has prompted the animal’s handler to resign amid administrative and criminal investigations, according to authorities.

Bart had been a patrol dog specializing in suspect apprehension, tracking, searches and drug detection before his handler found him dead inside his outdoor kennel on 19 September, Julian Wiser, the Madison county sheriff, said in a social media video announcement.

A veterinary necropsy of the two-and-a-half-year-old German shepherd found that he had died of heatstroke due to severe dehydration, with investigators learning Bart’s handler at the Madison sheriff’s office had not been home for about 36 hours while temperatures climbed to 101F (38.3C) and water was inaccessible to the canine.
In his video addressing the case, Wiser called Bart’s death “unfortunate and preventable”, and the sheriff also described himself as a former canine unit supervisor.

“This is … very sad and unfortunate,” Wiser said in the video on Friday. “We depend on our canines to help keep our community safe and our law enforcement officers, but our canines depend on us to take care of them.”
Bart’s handler was neither immediately identified by Wiser’s office nor formally charged with a crime. Wiser said the deputy resigned after being placed on administrative leave.

The sheriff added that his office had also served search warrants in connection with simultaneous internal and criminal investigations into Bart’s death. Wiser said resulting findings would be forwarded to prosecutors.
A survey published in the Police Practice and Research Journal found heatstroke to be the second-leading cause of death for police dogs in the line of duty, behind only gunfire.
In fact, heatstroke was responsible for one in five such deaths, according to the survey.

“Being left unattended and mechanical failures overwhelmingly (70.6%) characterized these heatstroke deaths,” said an abstract of the survey, which studied information on more than 400 canine deaths listed on the Officer Down Memorial Page website.
According to the survey’s abstract, “Summer months were also significantly implicated in increasing the odds of line-of-duty heatstroke deaths.”

articles.title: EXPLAINERS: What is the proposed Sierra Madre Mountain Range Authority?
articles.summary: The House Panel on Government Enterprises and Privatization tackled the substitute bill for 14 separate measures that propose the creation of the Sierra Madre Mountain Range Authority (SMMRA), with…

blocks.text: Published September 29, 2026 4:43pm

The House Panel on Government Enterprises and Privatization tackled the substitute bill for 14 separate measures that propose the creation of the Sierra Madre Mountain Range Authority (SMMRA), with one of the measures being filed by House Speaker Bojie Dy.
Dy had named the Sierra Madre measure a priority legislation by the Legislative-Executive Development Advisory Council (LEDAC).

According to Bukidnon First District Representative Jose Manuel Alba’s presentation, 130,000 hectares of Sierra Madre’s forest cover was reduced by logging from 2003 to 2020, while approved mining claims and applications cover 800,000 hectares across the mountain range corridor.
Alba, who serves as the chair of the bill’s technical working group, said the SMMRA is a “Unified Framework for Protection, Conservation, Resilience, and Sustainable Development.”
Spanning 540 kilometers across Cagayan to Quezon, Alba said there needed to be a new approach.

“Our current approach to protecting this mountain range is fundamentally broken because it is broken. We rely on isolated municipal zoning and project-by-project management. This bill drives a core policy shift towards landscape scale, science-based governance,” Alba said.
The new substitute bill proposes the creation of the SMMRA as a government-owned or -controlled corporation (GOCC) with its own charter, which will be attached to the Office of the President.
The SMMRA would be tasked with policy, planning and coordinating.

Alba explained the SMMRA will not replace any existing agency, but it will complement them instead. The Authority will not issue documents such as environmental compliance certificates, local permits and more.
At the head of the Authority will be a 17-member board of representatives from different sectors of government, specialists and private sector representatives.
The SMMRA will be tasked with creating a 25-year Sierra Madre Master plan, integrating land use planning, watershed protection and disaster risk reduction. It will be updated once every three years.
Alba said that extractive activities in the mountains must also be addressed.

“Upon the effectivity of this act, no new commercial mining application or agreement shall be authorized, anywhere within the geographical restriction of the Sierra Madre. Furthermore, existing commercial operations will face a mandatory, gradual phaseout,” Alba said.
Operators are mandated to submit a phaseout and restoration plan.
Since the proposed SMRRA is a GOCC, it is expected to become financially self-sustaining, so there will be a Sierra Madre fund.

Under the proposed measure, 10% of environmental fees charged by local government units will go to the SMMRA. It also has a share of penalty and forfeiture recoveries. The planned GOCC is also allowed to receive grants, and have other lawful sources of income.
These would help support scientific research, ecosystem accounting and more.
There will also be a “Sierra Madre Nature Credit System” where medium and big businesses who rely on the mountains will have an annual “nature credit purchase obligation.”
It is a regulatory debt that can be resolved by regularly purchasing nature credits.
“This market mechanism directly funnels corporate cash straight into the hands of local communities and forest stewards who do the actual protection network,” Alba said.
Compliance with this system is outcome based, not financial. They can pay these credits back by joining resilience investments or by banking on early warning systems.
The panel approved the bill and its accompanying committee report. — LA, GMA News

articles.title: Baste Duterte: 19 contracts granted by Davao to GenCorp 'not too many'
articles.summary: Davao City Mayor Sebastian "Baste" Duterte said Tuesday that the 19 government contracts that the Davao City government granted to GenCorp. Industries Inc., a declared asset of his sister and Vice…

blocks.text: Published September 29, 2026 4:36pm

Davao City Mayor Sebastian "Baste" Duterte said Tuesday that the 19 government contracts that the Davao City government granted to GenCorp. Industries Inc., a declared asset of his sister and Vice President Duterte, are "not too many."
The mayor, brother of Vice President Sara Duterte, made the testimony during Day 31 of the impeachment trial of the Vice President.

“19 [contracts] in a span of five years…I don’t think, hindi ganun karami, in the total volume,” the mayor said in his testimony during Day 31 of the impeachment trial of the Vice President after being asked by Senator judge Sherwin Gatchalian.
(That’s not too many.)
The Vice President declared GenCorp. Industries Inc. as one of her business interests in her Statement of Assets, Liabilities and Net Worth (SALN) in 2024 and 2025.
'Most qualified'
Baste Duterte also reiterated on Tuesday that he is unaware of his sister's investment in GenCorp.
“We do not discuss this [topic on her businesses],” the mayor said when asked by private prosecutor Theodore Te.

Gatchalian also quizzed the mayor if he was ever puzzled as to why GenCorp. kept on winning contracts with the Davao City government when there are so many caterers available, but Baste Duterte maintained everything was above board.

“He is behind me, and his answer was simply because they (GenCorp.) were the most qualified and they complied with all the requirements,” the mayor said, referring to Atty. Dwight Domingo who is the Davao City government’s Assistant City Administrator.

During the same proceeding, Baste Duterte confirmed that GenCorp. won a ₱8.4 million Davao City contract covering 60,000 servings of fried chicken, rice and bottled water without any competing bidder.
The Davao mayor, during questioning of private prosecutor Te, testified that the P8.4 million contract was a procurement for food and catering services requested by the City Mayor’s Office.

Asked by Gatchalian if he is aware of other companies whom GenCorp. beat in public and negotiated biddings for Davao City government contracts, Baste Duterte replied said he wasn’t aware of the profile of these companies while maintaining GenCorp. won the contracts fair and square.

“Hindi ko tinignan. Tinanong ko lang naman [si Atty. Domingo] kung tama ba yung proseso na pinagdaanan, May problema ba, may binaypas na law or whatever na process. Sinabi niya naman wala. Qualified naman and all under the law. That’s it,” the mayor added.

(I didn’t take a look at it. I just asked him if the process was allowed, if there was a problem, if a law was bypassed or any process was bypassed. I was told there was one, and that it is qualified, and the process [how it got the contract are] all under the law.)
'Not allowed'

In a separate press conference, the House prosecution panel said that it was never the number of contracts, but the supposed conflict of interest since the Vice President is a declared shareholder of the GenCorp. during the years that it got contracts from the Davao City government led by her brother.

“The issue here is the connection of the Vice President to GenCorp. Whether it is one, two, three, 19 contracts won by GenCorp., it is clear that such involvement to GenCorp by the Vice President is not allowed under the Constitution,” House prosecutor Joel Chua of Manila said.

Chua was referring to Article 7, Section 13 of the Constitution which states that “The President, Vice-President, the Members of the Cabinet, and their deputies or assistants shall not, during said tenure, directly or indirectly, practice any other profession, participate in any business, or be financially interested in any contract with, or in any franchise, or special privilege granted by the government or any subdivision, agency, or instrumentality thereof, including government-owned or controlled corporations or their subsidiaries. —VAL, GMA News

articles.title: Argentina's Milei threatens UK with international legal action over Falkland Islands oil project
articles.summary: A major offshore oil project is opening a new front in the Falklands sovereignty dispute, with Buenos Aires threatening legal action and sanctions against companies involved.

image.caption: Milei spoke at the UN General Assembly in New York days before threatening international legal action against the UK (FILE: 23/09/2026)Image: CNP/AdMedia/picture alliance

blocks.text: Argentine President Javier Milei on Monday gave the United Kingdom two weeks to halt an oil project near the Falkland Islands or face international legal action.
The potentially lucrative project has intensified the long-running sovereignty dispute as the islands prepare for oil production that could transform their small economy.
What has Argentina threatened to do?
Milei said Argentina would take the dispute to the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea in Hamburg if the UK did not halt the Sea Lion project within two weeks.

"I instructed the Foreign Ministry and our legal teams to initiate arbitration proceedings against the United Kingdom for the illegal sacking of our resources through the Sea Lion Project in the North Falklands Basin," Milei wrote on X.
"If within two weeks the United Kingdom does not stop the illegitimate exploitation, we will go to the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea," he added.
Argentina argues that Britain's authorization of oil exploration violates a UN resolution calling on both sides to refrain from unilateral actions while their sovereignty dispute remains unresolved.

blocks.caption: Port Stanley is the capital of the British-controlled Falkland Islands, which Argentina claims as the Malvinas (FILE: 07/10/2019)Image: Pablo Porciuncula/AFP

blocks.text: Milei has also threatened to bar companies involved in unauthorized oil exploration around the Falklands from operating in Argentina's oil and mining sectors.
His government has sent Argentina's Congress a bill proposing prison terms of up to 20 years for extracting resources around the islands without Argentine authorization.
Argentine authorities say they are investigating at least 60 companies and executives for possible violations.
What is the Sea Lion oil project?
Sea Lion is a major offshore oil field around 220 kilometers (137 miles) north of the Falkland Islands.
The project is being developed by Israel's Navitas Petroleum and Britain's Rockhopper Exploration under licenses issued by the Falkland Islands authorities.
Oil production is expected to begin in 2028.
The companies have rejected Argentina's objections, saying they hold valid licenses for the project.

blocks.caption: Britain and Argentina fought a 10-week war over the Falkland Islands in 1982 after Argentine forces invaded the British-controlled territory [FILE: 1982]Image: PA/empics/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: The UK has also defended the right of the Falkland Islanders to develop their natural resources.
Why are the Falkland Islands disputed?
The Falkland Islands have been under British control since 1833, but Argentina claims sovereignty over the archipelago, which it calls the Malvinas.
Argentina invaded the islands in 1982, triggering a 10-week war with the UK.
The conflict killed 649 Argentine military personnel, 255 British service members and three islanders before British forces retook the territory.
The UK says the islanders have the right to determine their own future.
In a 2013 referendum, 99.8% of voters backed remaining a British Overseas Territory, with turnout of about 92%.
Argentina rejects the referendum and maintains its sovereignty claim.

articles.title: Impeachment court admonishes prosecution’s Tolosa over press briefing remarks
articles.summary: Tolosa says he disagrees, but will respect the impeachment court's decision

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines – Prosecution panel spokesman Jay Tolosa said on Tuesday, September 29, that the impeachment court in Vice President Sara Duterte’s trial has admonished him over public comments that were previously flagged for potential violation of its sub judice rule.
Tolosa said the ruling did not explicitly say that the admonition was tantamount to a first offense, but if it were, a subsequent violation by Tolosa would result in a P30,000 fine.

“I respectfully disagree with the admonition. There is no finding that I violated the rule. While I respectfully disagree, I respect the authority of the impeachment court as an institution, and with that, I will not belabor the point and I will, of course, respect that admonition and be even more careful in giving statements moving forward,” Tolosa said in a press conference.

The decision came after the court compelled Tolosa to explain his remarks made during a September 8 press conference. There, he said, the prosecution’s evidentiary targets have been met, that it was clear to the Commission on Audit that Duterte’s offices violated rules on confidential spending, and that the vice president cannot say she will not take the witness stand and invoke her right against self-incrimination.
The court’s sub judice rule bars parties from making comments in public pertaining to the merits of the trial.

Tolosa, in his reply to the show-cause order issued to him, asserted that his comments made to the media were procedural matters outside the sub judice rule of the impeachment court, and were just accurate reiterations of matters already placed on record.
Tolosa is among the four spokespersons of the prosecution team, but is the only one who is bound by the sub judice rule.

Tolosa is a seasoned litigator. The UST alumnus represented American soldier Joseph Pemberton, who was convicted of homicide in the killing of Filipino transgender woman Jennifer Laude in October 2014, and also counseled Philippine Airlines and the local affiliate of Fortune 500 company Philip Morris International. – Rappler.com

articles.title: UK: US government questions bail for Fairford base suspects
articles.summary: The US government sees "the hand of a foreign actor" in the security scare at RAF Fairford, a hub for US heavy bombers in Europe. Donald Trump criticized the suspects being released on bail amid…

image.caption: Police sealed off the area near the air base amid Sunday's operation Image: Alastair Grant/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: The US government has described the security alert over the weekend at the RAF Fairford base in southern England as a "very serious situation," thanking UK authorities for their cooperation.
But President Donald Trump and Secretary of State Marco Rubio also both questioned the move to grant the five suspects bail under strict conditions as investigations against them continue.

RAF Fairford is a major military air field fairly close to the south coast of England. It's a rare European base from which the US operates heavy bombers, with the range to reach Iran amid the current conflict in the Gulf.

blocks.caption: Long-range US bombers have operated out of Fairford since it was set up near the end of World War IIImage: Alastair Grant/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: What did Rubio and Trump say about the case?

Marco Rubio said in an interview with Fox News that while there was much he could not say on air for now, the security scare during which five young men were detained constituted a very serious situation.

"It's one that clearly involves the hand of a foreign actor. I won't get into great detail about that yet," he said, without mentioning Iran until a later point in the interview in a more hypothetical context.

"I think it ties us to the reality here, and that is we are dealing with elements in the world, and in the case of Iran, for example, who have openly threatened to attack American interests globally," Rubio said.
The Iranian Embassy in London, meanwhile, said that it "categorically rejects and strongly condemns the recent unfounded and malicious speculations" of Iranian involvement.
Rubio also echoed President Donald Trump in saying that "a lot of people are disturbed by the news that some of these people have released on bail."
Trump had mentioned the issue in comments to reporters in the White House earlier on Monday.
"I will tell you, I would have said, 'Don't let them have bail.' I'm surprised that they released them. I wouldn't have done that," he said.
UK releases air base plot suspects
What have British investigators said about the case?

Five men in their 20s, all from the London area and with British citizenship, were arrested on Sunday in the vicinity of the air base, which is in a rural area roughly two hours' drive west of the capital. They were wearing face coverings.
Police seized three "suspicious" white vans and evacuated around 85 households in the vicinity, bringing in bomb disposal teams.

Locals were able to return home on Monday, and preliminary reports from the British Press Association and others suggestd the materials in the vehicles were not viable explosives, but counterterrorism and explosives experts continued to examine the scene.

The head of UK Counter Terrorism Policing, Assistant Commissioner Laurence Taylor, acknowledged the "significant interest in whether the current geopolitical context has a bearing on this incident," and said investigators were considering "every possible angle."
One of these angles, he said, was the possibility "that this may be actively committed by proxies or individuals either knowingly or unknowingly working on behalf of a foreign state."
Taylor said that the men had been released under stringent conditions, and that granting them bail did not in any signify an end to investigations against them.
Defense Secretary Wes Streeting said that decisions like granting bail were operational matters for police and prosecutors, not politicians.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham chaired a security meeting known as Cobra, after the secure Cabinet Office Briefing Room A that hosts such sessions, on Monday evening.

blocks.caption: Even prior to Sunday's deployment, security was already tighter than usual at sensitive UK facilities like RAF FairfordImage: Toby Shepheard/REUTERS

blocks.text: What is RAF Fairford?
RAF Fairford is a large military airbase not far north of Swindon in Gloucestershire, west of London.

It's a base for US heavy bombers in Europe and has been used as a launch point for operations involving long-range B-52s in a series of conflicts in recent decades including both Iraq wars, the NATO bombing of the former Yugoslavia, and most recently in a limited capacity in Iran this year.
Residents in the Cotswolds region had noted an increased security presence and activity at the base amid the conflict, as is often observable around such bases during such periods.

Because of the longstanding close military ties — and very often infrastructure set up during World War II when Nazi Germany occupied much of Europe — southern England is home to a string of airbases also used by the US military.

articles.title: 1 in 8 cancer cases worldwide are caused by infections, study finds

image.caption: A health worker shows vials of human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccine during a campaign aiming to protect girls from cervical cancer, in Karachi, Pakistan, in 2025. The virus causes 100 per cent of cases of cervical cancer. (Fareed Khan/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: For many people, sun exposure, smoking and family history are the first thoughts that come to mind regarding cancer risk factors. While infections are rarely high on the list, new research shows one in eight cancers worldwide are actually caused by them.

These viruses, bacteria and other microbes are the focus of a new paper published Monday in The Lancet Oncology that linked an estimated 2.3 million new cancer cases in 2024 — 12 per cent of all new cases — to these infectious agents.

A team of researchers at The International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC), an arm of the World Health Organization, conducted the study. They found the largest number of cancer cases attributed to infections globally were caused by the bacterium Helicobacter pylori, which can increase the risk of stomach cancer and accounted for 760,000 cases, predominantly in eastern Asia.

Human papillomavirus (HPV) followed close behind. HPV, which causes 100 per cent of cervical cancer cases and also anal, vulvar, vaginal, penile and some head and neck cancers, accounted for nearly 750,000 new cases globally, with high rates in sub-Saharan Africa. Hepatitis B virus (HBV) and hepatitis C virus (HCV) were also linked to a significant number of liver cancer cases.
For the first time, researchers linked even more cancers to infections, expanding their list to include 16 additional ones.
Gary Clifford, a cancer epidemiologist and study co-author based in Lyon, France, said the science has advanced significantly.

"There's been new infectious agents identified in this time as being cancer-causing, and even the infectious agents that we knew about in the past, the evidence has increased about the number of different cancers that they can cause," he said.
Some of those new infectious agents included HIV and its link to cervical cancer, and a very rare virus called Merkel cell polyomavirus that can lead to an aggressive form of skin cancer.

To come up with numbers, researchers first examined which infections cause cancer, then calculated what fraction of these cancers can be linked to specific infections and applied those calculations to global databases of new cancer cases.

Another significant shift is the recognition of the role of Epstein-Barr virus (EBV). EBV was linked to about 260,000 cases globally in 2024, and can lead to nasopharyngeal cancer, some gastric cancers and Hodgkin's lymphoma.
"That's quite a big burden of cancer caused by Epstein-Barr virus that was not counted in the past, but is now recognized," Clifford said.

Epstein-Barr virus is also a key risk factor in developing multiple sclerosis, and unlike some of the other infections that have vaccines or antibiotic treatments, there are no available tools to fight against it.

items: New findings 'strongly suggest' Epstein-Barr virus may help trigger multiple sclerosis

blocks.text: "The fact that we're seeing Epstein-Barr has caused all these chronic diseases — it's increasingly becoming a target that people need to focus on for prevention," he said.

The global report highlights vast regional differences, mostly driven by historical disparities, researchers said. High-income countries that established cancer screening and vaccination programs over the last few decades are doing much better compared to lower- and medium-resourced countries where access to prevention and treatment is limited.
"We really still have a lot of work to do implementing things that we know work and we've known for a long time but haven't really made it into all populations in the world," Clifford said.
In North America, the burden of cancer-causing infections is much lower, but H. pylori and HPV are the most common sources.
Infections causing cancer in Canada

In Canada, according to a 2019 study, the rate of cancers attributable to infections was estimated to be at four per cent. Karena Volesky, an epidemiologist in Montreal, led the Canadian research team while at McGill University.
"It tells us how important each of the 12 infections are," Volesky said of the new global numbers.
While there is a lower prevalence of these forms of infections in Canada, her study estimated these infections lead to more than 7,000 cancer diagnoses each year.
Doctors urge Canadians to get HPV vaccine to prevent cervical cancer
"HPV is certainly an infection that we're keeping an eye on in Canada," said Elizabeth Holmes, the director of health policy at the Canadian Cancer Society.
Holmes said cervical cancer rates had been steadily declining in Canada due to robust childhood vaccination programs, but plateaued last year.
"That's certainly a concern — that we might not meet our goal of elimination of cervical cancer by 2040 unless those rates start to decline again," she said.

items: Cervical cancer rates show a 'concerning plateau,' according to new Canadian Cancer Society data

blocks.text: Human papillomavirus is transmitted through sexual contact, but the HPV vaccine protects against the most common forms of infection that can cause cancer.
Canada's cervical cancer elimination plan aims to increase vaccination rates to 90 per cent, increase screening rates to 90 per cent and ensure timely followup care after screening.
"Right now, only about five provinces are above 80 per cent, and I think at least one is as low as 66 per cent," Holmes said.
The stomach bacteria that can lead to cancer

The infection leading to the most cancer cases is Helicobacter pylori, a bacterium first discovered in the early 1980s that mainly leads to gastric cancers. While the research found the highest burden in eastern Asia in countries like Japan, South Korea and China, it's a problem here, too.
"It's a horrible disease to die from," said Dr. Paul Moayyedi, a leading researcher and gastroenterologist at McMaster University. About 2,000 Canadians die every year from stomach cancer.

Moayyedi wants to see a universal screening program for the bacterium, which can be detected through a blood or breath test, stool sample or endoscopy and treated with a combination of antibiotics over a two-week period.

Helicobacter pylori is associated with crowded living conditions and poor sanitation in childhood. While most people with it can live a long life without any issues, if left untreated, it can cause ulcers and stomach cancer for some.

Moayyedi said stomach cancers may not be seen as high priority compared to other types of cancers, but believes screening programs for those at high risk, such as people with a family history of stomach cancers or First Nations communities, would save lives.
"In consultation with the elders of local communities it would be important to at least offer those groups screening if they would want it," he said.

articles.title: How a rape rumour sent an Indian university into turmoil and emptied hostels
articles.summary: Police are trying to verify whether a female student was raped at Lovely Professional University (LPU).

blocks.text: Image source, Pardeep Sharma/BBC
Some violent protesters allegedly torched police cars parked on the highway on Sunday
ByZoya Mateen & Azadeh Moshiri
BBC News, Delhi
One of India's largest private universities has suspended classes after an unverified allegation that a female student was raped on campus set off protests that descended into violence.

Police say they have registered a case and are trying to verify whether last week's alleged rape at Lovely Professional University (LPU) did happen. The university has categorically denied the allegation.

Police say no student has come forward to say she was assaulted, investigators have yet to identify the alleged victim or the perpetrator, and CCTV footage examined so far has yielded no evidence of an attack.
But rumours on student WhatsApp groups led to unrest over the weekend at the sprawling 600-acre university in Punjab that draws students from India and abroad.

Founded in 2005 by a family whose business began with a small sweet shop, LPU has grown into a largely self-contained world of hostels and lecture halls, with thousands of young people living on campus.

Images and videos showed vehicles in flames, crowds filling a major highway and police wielding canes as unrest spilled beyond the university gates. Police vehicles were damaged, officers injured and parts of the campus was vandalised.
By Monday, the highway had reopened and the campus was calmer, but heavily policed.

University authorities described the claims circulating on social media as false and baseless, but it did little to reassure students with hostels emptying within hours. Key exams were postponed and students were allowed to go home.
Following demands from protesting students, police registered a rape case against "an unidentified person" and formed a seven-member special investigation team, or SIT, to investigate.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Lovely Professional University has suspended classes for 10 days amid violent protests

blocks.text: Lovely Professional University has suspended classes for 10 days amid violent protests
What happened?
The unrest began in the early hours of 27 September, when word spread that a female student had been raped in or near one of the university's hostels a few days earlier.

The suspect was variously described - by students and in media reports - as a plumber, painter or construction worker. Some students said the assault had occurred on 23 September and accused the university of failing to act after being informed.
BBC Punjabi found that messages about the allegation had circulated through WhatsApp groups. As they travelled, crowds gathered.

Hundreds eventually spilled on to National Highway 44, a major route between Delhi and Punjab, blocking traffic for more than 15 hours. By Sunday evening, university property had been damaged, objects set alight and stones thrown at police vehicles. Videos showed police striking protesters with canes, although police later denied carrying out a baton-charge.
Behind the gates, students described a night of fear.

"We were sitting with knives and scissors," Arya, a student, told BBC Punjabi. Students had been told to lock themselves inside their rooms, she said, while people knocked on their doors. "We were just thinking that somehow this night would pass and we would get out of here."
Police later arrived and made them feel safer, she said. By the next day, she wanted to leave. "Our parents also want us to just get out of here."

blocks.caption: Image caption, Arya, a student at the college, says they thought about nothing but leaving the campus on the night of violence

blocks.text: Image source, BBC Punjabi
Arya, a student at the college, says they thought about nothing but leaving the campus on the night of violence
So why have police lodged a case?
Because that was among the protesters' central demands.

"The students have been demanding that an FIR [First Information Report] is to be registered, but the students could not provide us with any victim's name," senior police official Naveen Singla told the BBC.
Police nevertheless registered an FIR under India's rape law against an unidentified person. An FIR formally records an allegation for investigation; it does not establish that a crime occurred.
Singla said investigators had also begun examining CCTV footage. The preliminary search, he told the BBC, had so far shown no outsider entering a room.
"As of now, it can't be verified that rape has happened or not," he said.
But they are continuing to examine the footage.

"The campus is quite large, so we haven't been able to see all the cameras yet," Sinha told reporters on Monday. "We have initially checked the places that the students had mentioned, but we will get to the bottom of this."

blocks.caption: Image caption, Protesting students had earlier blocked a nearby highway which was opened later on Monday

blocks.text: Protesting students had earlier blocked a nearby highway which was opened later on Monday
Why did the protests grow so large?
It is difficult to say. What began with an allegation of rape quickly became a broader protest over security, the university's response and, eventually, the violence itself.

There was also growing uncertainty over who was on the campus. Some students insisted the demonstrations had begun peacefully and blamed outsiders for at least some of the violence. Others told BBC Punjabi of seeing masked or unfamiliar people inside the university.
"We were really scared," said Pawan, a student. "It became a complete battlefield."

Another student, Aniket Singh, said outsiders had entered a women's hostel and knocked on doors claiming to be police officers. Police have since confirmed that outsiders were among the crowds, but said they were still trying to establish who they were and what role they played.
Amid that confusion, the university's attempt to dispel the rape allegation produced a controversy of its own.
On Monday, LPU released a video of three women living in the hostel room that had been linked to the alleged assault. They said nothing had happened there and asked people to stop disturbing them.

The same students later alleged in another video that university officials had instructed them what to say, edited the recording and posted it without their consent. Those claims have not been independently verified. LPU has not commented on the students' allegations.

Another claim circulating during the protests sought to connect the alleged rape with the recent suicide of a female LPU student from Telangana state. Police say investigations into her death had already begun and there is no verified evidence linking the two cases.

blocks.caption: Image caption, There is heavy police presence around the university campus since the unrest

blocks.text: Image source, ANI
There is heavy police presence around the university campus since the unrest
What is happening now?
For now, life on campus has been interrupted. Regular classes have been suspended for 10 days and exams postponed. Students have been asked to return home after consulting their parents or guardians.
Those who are staying have been advised to stay in their residences and avoid further unrest.
The Punjab State Women's Commission has also sought the FIR, details of the investigation and information about arrangements for students' safety.
The investigation now has two separate questions to answer: whether there is evidence of the assault that set the protests in motion? And who was responsible for the violence that followed?

Addressing the students on Monday, LPU's pro-chancellor Rashmi Mittal said she was hurt that despite the university's many channels for students to raise concerns, they had instead "believed the rumour that was spreading". She also alleged that outsiders had joined the unrest.
"I feel students can't do this," she said.
Additional reporting by Harmandeep Singh, BBC Punjabi
