articles.title: France: Student protests over conditions at French high schools fuel political clashes
articles.summary: Over 160 people were arrested and dozens injured after student protests in France descended into violence. With a presidential election approaching, senior politicians are pointing fingers at each…

image.caption: The student protests began in the Ile-de-France region around the capital, Paris, but on Monday spread to other regionsImage: CLPRESS/abaca/picture alliance

blocks.text: Student protests spread to high schools across France on Monday, resulting in dozens of injuries, over 160 arrests and arguments between senior politicians — a day ahead of a nationwide strike by public sector workers and seven months ahead of the presidential election.

Teenagers at French lycées (equivalent to US high schools) have been blockading their schools since last week in protest at overcrowded classes, heavy workloads, poor quality learning materials and teacher shortages.
The movement began in the Ile-de-France region around the capital, Paris, but on Monday spread to other regions including Lille in the north, Marseille in the south and Sedan in the east.
Video footage on French media showed student protesters lighting flares and firing fireworks, even inside a school building, while police officers responded with tear gas.

blocks.caption: Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu called the 'escalation' of the situation 'irresponsible'Image: Adnan Farzat/NurPhoto/picture alliance

blocks.text: French student protests: what have politicians said?
As of Monday night, French Interior Minister Laurent Nunez reported incidents at around 180 establishments resulting in 164 arrests and injuries to 12 students, three teachers and 12 police officers.
He acknowledged that the "difficulties of high schools must be heard and addressed" but said: "This wasn't about making demands, it was really violence in its purest form."
He added that "a number of individuals … were masked, equipped with fireworks in tubes and projectiles [and] clearly wanted to confront the internal security forces."

Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu called the "escalation" of the situation "irresponsible" and said: "Fireworks, fires, violence near high schools: nothing justifies endangering students, staff, or police officers."
'Hands off our youth!' French politicians clash over protests

Education Minister Edouard Geffray said that the protests, which he described as a "classic high school student movement," were being exploited by violent elements — and took aim at the left-wing La France Insoumise (France Unbowed or LFI) party and its presidential candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon.
"There is a political hijacking of the blockades by elected officials from France Unbowed," he said.
Earlier on Monday, Mélenchon had accused the government of implementing a "crackdown" with "obvious racist undertones."
"Hands off our youth!" he wrote on social media, while encouraging LFI activists and officials to support the protests wherever they could.

Prime Minister Lecornu called the accusation of racism "an insult" and accused Mélenchon of "racializing a debate about student security and adding to division where a responsible politician should be looking to restore calm."
In the Parisian suburb of Saint-Denis, the LFI-run local council called the students' demands "legitimate" and published a statement reading:

"Let [the authorities] come and talk to [the students] and see for themselves whether the youth are being instrumentalized, or whether they are simply capable of thinking, organizing themselves and defending their own study conditions and their future."
France: The camps under Paris bridges
France: strikes — and an election — to come

The Union Syndicale Lycéenne, the French union that defends the interests of high school students, said it would urge a nationwide blockade of schools on Tuesday — coinciding with planned strike action by public sector workers.
French primary school teachers' unions said they expected some 40% of teachers to be off work on Tuesday.

With a key presidential election only seven months away and incumbent President Emmanuel Macron constitutionally barred from standing for a third term, French politicians from across the ideological spectrum are seeking issues that resonate with voters.
Mélenchon, a 75-year-old veteran anti-capitalist who finished third in the 2022 presidential election, is popular among younger, left-leaning voters.

His LFI party was one of the left-wing outfits which joined the Nouveau Front Populaire (New Popular Front or NFP) coalition in 2024 to oppose the far-right Rassemblement National (National Rally or RN) in legislative elections.
The coalition beat the RN but the elections produced a divided parliament which has been dogged by political deadlock and votes of no-confidence.

Prime Minister Lecornu is still trying to build enough support to pass a 2027 state budget, but his government is besieged by opponents who are unwilling to accept spending cuts while energy costs continue to rise.
Leo makes first official papal visit to France in 18 years

OpenAI has scrapped the release of GPT-6.1 Astra, a next-generation artificial intelligence model planned for an October debut, after internal testing found the system did not meet the company's ‌safety and alignment standards, the ChatGPT maker confirmed on Monday.
Company says internal testing determined GPT-6.1 Astra didn't meet safety standards

OpenAI has ​warned that Astra, its flagship GPT-6 model, can at times evade human oversight, while the company and rivals such as ​Anthropic have faced scrutiny over experimental AI systems that breached ⁠safeguards, including an ⁠OpenAI model that accessed Australia's health system ‌database.

The Wall Street Journal reported earlier in the day that OpenAI had abandoned plans to launch the model, which was expected to be integrated into ChatGPT and Codex and was designed to handle ⁠more complex tasks without human assistance.
OpenAI’s AI went rogue at least 4 times. This researcher caught 3 of them | Hanomansing Tonight

The Journal reported that GPT-6.1 Astra also showed higher levels of deception than its predecessor in internal testing, including instances in ‌which it did not always accurately disclose what actions it had taken.

articles.title: Lost songs from iconic Australian rockstar found in garage
articles.summary: Divinyls frontwoman Chrissy Amphlett recorded the songs with Split Enz's Tim Finn in 1998.

blocks.text: More than a decade after her death, the voice of Australian rock icon Chrissy Amphlett will be heard like never before after three lost songs were discovered in a garage.

The trailblazing frontwoman of rock band Divinyls, Amphlett's trademark husky voice and charismatic stage presence brought the world the 1990 number one track I Touch Myself as well as earlier hits Pleasure and Pain (1985) and Boys in Town (1981).

Years before her 2013 death, Amphlett recorded three songs with Tim Finn, former lead singer of New Zealand's Split Enz, in 1998. The tracks were thought to be lost until Finn found them in his garage in 2023.
On Friday, the songs will be released in an EP titled Some Times.
In an interview with Australian Story, a documentary programme by national broadcaster ABC, Finn recalled the 1998 recording session with Amphlett in Sydney.
"It was a good time for us to meet because she was looking for something new, something different in her life musically," Finn said.

Around that time, Amphlett had split with fellow band member, guitarist Mark McEntee after a tumultuous relationship and was growing close to drummer Charley Drayton, according to the documentary. The pair would later marry.
Over several days, he and Amphlett wrote a trio of songs and headed into the studio to record them, with Drayton on the drums.
"She was so focused," Finn said. "She just wanted to get it right... I was in the presence of great talent, great charisma."
In a social media post on Monday about the 1998 session, Finn said he had reached out to Amphlett having been a great admirer of her work.
"We hadn't met previously but instantly felt a bond, a camaraderie of shared history as ex-lead singers of two brilliant bands," Finn wrote on Monday.
When the session wrapped up, Finn took the recordings home and planned to work on it, but "they were never fully realised".
In 2023, Drayton contacted Finn, about the 1998 recordings.

"I thought they were lost to the universe but remarkably found the two-inch tape in my garage," Finn wrote in the post, describing the songs as "incredibly important to me, Charley and those close to Chrissy".
"It was still in perfect condition and we are now able to share these songs with you."

articles.title: Evicted Spanish pensioner can move back home, lawyer says
articles.summary: The eviction of Maricarmen Abascal, 87, prompted large-scale protests across Spain.

blocks.text: Image source, NurPhoto via Getty Images
The eviction of Maricarmen Abascal prompted large-scale protests across Spain
ByVictoria Bourne
BBC News
An evicted elderly disabled woman, who became symbolic of Spain's housing crisis, will be able to return to her home in Madrid, according to her lawyer.
Maricarmen Abascal, 87, was forcibly removed on a stretcher from her apartment of more than 70 years on 23 September. She was admitted to hospital after the eviction.
The eviction led to widespread anger across Spain, and prime minister Pedro Sanchez has promised housing relief measures when his cabinet meets on Tuesday.

Abascal's lawyer, Beatriz Duro, told a press conference there had been "goodwill from both parties" and that she would pay a similar amount of rent under a new contract, averting a significant price hike.

blocks.caption: Maricarmen Abascal, an 87-year-old disabled woman is carried out of the building on a stretcher on September 23, 2026 in Madrid

blocks.text: Image source, Getty Images
Abascal's father first rented the property in 1956 and she continued as the tenant after her parents died, during which time there was a cap on the rent.
Investment firm Urbagestión, which bought the property in 2018, increased the rent from €500 per month (£428; $572) to €2,650 (£2,280; $3,020).
The company later offered to reduce this to €1,650 however she was still unable to pay this with her monthly pension of €1,350.
Three previous attempts to evict her were blocked by the courts.

Her case triggered nationwide protests and tens of thousands of people to march through the Spanish capital on Saturday to object to the eviction and to demand stronger protection for tenants in the face of a housing shortage and soaring rents.
Watch: Spain’s housing crisis in focus after eviction of 87-year-old woman
Duro said the agreement, yet to be signed, was the "result of the social mobilisation".
She added that Abascal, who is being treated for exhaustion, would sign the deal when she feels better.
Supporters called it a victory but promised to continue their fight to prevent similar evictions, and to press for more affordable housing.
The Bank of Spain estimates the country is short of 700,000 homes, based on the gap between demand and new construction.
Pedro Sanchez's Socialist Party, which lacks a majority in Parliament, is hoping to pass a law to appease public outrage.

articles.title: OpenAI scraps rollout of new model over safety concerns
articles.summary: The AI giant's safety chief said the model 'didn't quite meet the bar' of the firm's security standards.

blocks.text: OpenAI will not release its next-generation model - GPT-6.1 Astra - due to safety concerns, the ChatGPT-maker confirmed on Tuesday.
The AI system - which performs tasks like browsing the web and using apps by itself - "didn't quite meet the bar" of the company's standards, Saachi Jain, head of safety systems at OpenAI, said.

In recent weeks, top AI leaders including OpenAI's Sam Altman and Anthropic boss Dario Amodei have urged the industry to slow the pace of development due to concerns about risks associated with the technology.
The debate around those risks has intensified in recent weeks after models developed by top AI firms were involved in a number of incidents.
OpenAI's decision, first reported by the Wall Street Journal, is a rare instance of a major AI developer pulling a new release over safety concerns.
The latest model fell short in terms of "staying within scope and authorisation, and how it communicates back to the user about the type of work it's done," Jain said.

"We want to make sure our model development is safe no matter whether that's in the company, or when we ship it to users. But when we ship it to users, we have an extremely high bar in terms of safety and alignment," she added.

The flagship GPT-6 Astra agentic model was released in September and specialises in complex reasoning and executing tasks autonomously. OpenAI said it was the result of "years of research and big bets".
The company's security controls have come under intense scrutiny after several high-profile incidents involving its technology.

Last week, Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese announced that a rogue OpenAI agent had hacked into a government website in June and accessed private data in what experts said was the first known case of its kind in the world.

In July, OpenAI said its AI systems had accessed the internet and hacked into open-source developer hub Hugging Face, prompting researchers and officials to call for tighter controls over the technology.
On Monday, AI chip giant Nvidia released a set of software safety tools for autonomous AI platforms - called agents - that it said could have prevented the Hugging Face hack.
One of the new tools uses hardware features in Nvidia's chips to contain agents.
Nvidia boss Jensen Huang has largely dismissed calls for tighter AI regulations, arguing that rogue agents are an engineering problem that can be solved.
Nvidia agreed to buy Hugging Face for $12.9bn (£9.74bn) earlier this month.

articles.title: Israel's Netanyahu holds secret meeting with UAE president
articles.summary: After confirming a rare meeting, Netanyahu's office has denied suggestions that the Israeli prime minister requested that Abu Dhabi deny reports that it had warned Israel about an impending Hamas…

image.caption: It is the first time that the UAE has officially acknowledged a meeting between the two leadersImage: picture alliance

blocks.text: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu secretly met with the president of the United Arab Emirates (UAE), Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan, in Abu Dhabi on Sunday, both governments confirmed late on Monday.
"The two sides discussed bilateral relations between the UAE and Israel and ways to strengthen and develop them," read an Emirati statement.
Netanyahu's office said the visit "focused on strengthening relations between the two countries and on regional challenges."

The secret trip came weeks after a bombshell Israeli media report that the UAE president had warned Netanyahu about an imminent threat from the Palestinian militant group Hamas ahead of the deadly attack on Israel on October 7, 2023 — a warning which the Israeli premier allegedly failed to pass on to security services.
Indeed, Israeli broadcaster Channel 12 reported on Monday that the purpose of Netanyahu's visit had been to request that Sheikh Mohamed deny having given such a warning.
Netanyahu's office denied that the prime minister had made any such request, just as it had also denied the original report.
Netanyahu files complaint against Israeli broadcaster

Earlier on Monday, before the confirmation of Netanyahu's trip, Israel's domestic security service Shin Bet filed a complaint against Channel 12, accusing it of violating censorship rules by reporting the visit before the prime minister had returned to Israel.

"This evening, Shin Bet filed a complaint with the Chief Military Censor, demanding that Channel 12 be prosecuted to the fullest extent of the law following a severe censorship violation," read a statement from Netanyahu's office.

It noted that the report had been made public while the premier's plane was still outside Israeli airspace and therefore "endangered the lives of the prime minister and his wife, as well as the delegation, which included the head of the Mossad" spy agency and other top security officials.
How the Iran war has deepened Saudi-UAE rivalry
Israel and the UAE: diplomatic relations

Sheikh Mohamed's hosting of Netanyahu was a significant development at a time when the Israeli leader is seen by many across the Middle East as the chief propagator of the war in Gaza, which has seen over 70,000 Palestinians killed — many of them civilians.
It is also the first time that the UAE has officially acknowledged a meeting between the two leaders after denying reports of a previous Netanyahu trip in May.
The UAE is one of only a handful of Arab nations which maintain official diplomatic ties with Israel after signing the Abraham Accords during US President Donald Trump's first term in 2020.
The UAE condemned the Hamas attack on Israel on October 7, 2023 as a "serious and grave escalation" and said it was "appalled" by reports of Israeli citizens being taken hostage.
But relations have also been strained by Israel's subsequent war in Gaza, with the UAE denouncing "ongoing Israeli violations" in the Palestinian enclave.

Nevertheless, Israel reportedly deployed Iron Dome air defense systems, together with personnel to operate them, to the UAE during the war against Iran, as the Gulf state faced retaliatory attacks from Tehran.

articles.title: Sign before praying: A new conversion law is affecting churchgoers in Indian state
articles.summary: A new anti-conversion law in Maharashtra is raising questions about faith, choice and freedom.

blocks.text: Sign before praying: A new conversion law is affecting churchgoers in Indian state
Image source, AFP via Getty Images
A new anti-conversion law in Maharashtra has sparked fears among Christians
ByJanhavee MooleBBC Marathi, Mumbai and Zoya MateenBBC News, Delhi
Some churches in and around India's financial capital Mumbai have begun asking worshippers to give a declaration in writing - "I came here to pray of my own free will."

Visitors write down their names, sometimes add an ID card number, and sign to say that nobody forced or enticed them to attend church. The forms, a copy of which the BBC has seen, have no official standing. Churches keep them in case a prayer meeting is challenged and its organisers are accused of trying to convert those inside.
The practice began at some churches in late August, just before a new law against religious conversion took effect in Maharashtra state, of which Mumbai is the capital.

The law prohibits religious conversions brought about by force, fraud, coercion or inducement. It also requires people who want to convert voluntarily to notify authorities in advance. An unlawful conversion can lead to a prison sentence of up to seven years, rising to 10 for a repeat offence.
Maharashtra's government says the law protects people, particularly those who are socially or economically vulnerable, from being forced or deceived into changing their religion.

But critics say its broad definitions, severe penalties and scrutiny of even voluntary conversions risk drawing the state and the police into one of the most private decisions a person can make. The state government did not respond to the BBC's repeated requests for comment.

While the law applies to all religions, the anxiety is being felt most deeply at places where minorities, especially Christians, worship. At the heart of the debate is a long-running tension over allegations, usually made by right-wing groups, about people being coerced or induced to change their religion for benefits.
Devdan Tribhuvan has seen some of that anxiety up close.

A fourth-generation Christian in Vasai, a suburb of Mumbai, he is part of an organisation that provides legal aid to Christians in and around the city. In recent months, he says, people have increasingly approached him not about court cases, but with accounts of disrupted prayer meetings and questions about what they are still free to do.
Some have described strangers walking into churches and questioning those inside: "What is your name? Why are you here? Has anyone offered you something?"

blocks.caption: Image caption, People from all religions visit the famous Mount Mary Church in Mumbai

blocks.text: Image source, Getty Images
People from all religions visit the famous Mount Mary Church in Mumbai
The questions can become more pointed, Tribhuvan said, when a worshipper has a name that does not sound Christian: "Has anyone forced you to come? Has anyone offered you an inducement?"
Many who contact him are not looking to take legal action. They want to know whether simply gathering to pray could leave them vulnerable to an accusation of conversion.

In July, an investigation by The Indian Express, external documented five disruptions of Christian prayer meetings around Mumbai between April and July. Nine police cases followed - seven against worshippers or prayer organisers, and two against members of the Hindu nationalist group Bajrang Dal. Police did not respond to detailed questions about the cases or the action taken.
"Is gathering for prayer itself conversion?" Tribhuvan asks.

In Mumbai, Tribhuvan's question carries particular weight. The city grew by drawing people from across India and beyond, bringing their gods and rituals with them. A church bell can sound within earshot of a mosque's call to prayer; a shrine belonging to one faith can draw followers of another.

People of many faiths make their way to the Muslim shrine Haji Ali. Hindus light candles at Mount Mary, a Catholic basilica overlooking the city. Crowds fill the streets around Lalbaug during the Hindu festival of Ganesh Chaturthi and stream to Siddhivinayak temple throughout the year.

Maharashtra is the latest of more than a dozen states to restrict religious conversion. The laws differ, but their reach has expanded in recent years, particularly in states governed by Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party. Several are being challenged before the Supreme Court.

Behind that expansion lie claims long made by Hindu nationalist groups, that Christians use money, schooling or medical care to draw poor and tribal communities away from Hinduism, and that Muslim men court Hindu women to convert them - an alleged conspiracy they call "love jihad."

blocks.caption: Image caption, A bunch of anti-conversion laws in Indian states have made interfaith marriages more challenging

blocks.text: Image source, Reuters
A bunch of anti-conversion laws in Indian states have made interfaith marriages more challenging

Critics say such accusations have fuelled harassment of Christian prayer meetings and interfaith couples, and that the laws give those making them a way to draw the police into questions of prayer, marriage and belief.
Maharashtra's government says the new law leaves people free to convert by choice, while addressing what it says is a rise in forced conversions that existing laws have failed to curb.
Critics question where it draws the line between force and choice.

"We do not support forceful conversions, if any," said Samsuddin Tamboli, president of the Muslim Satyashodhak Mandal (Muslim Truth-seeking Society), a reformist organisation. His concern is what the law counts as inducement.

Its definition of "allurement" includes employment, free education at a religious institution, a promise of marriage, a "better lifestyle" and "divine healing". Even glorifying one religion over another can fall within it.
"The definition has been kept so vague that almost any benefit accruing to a person can be considered or argued to be an allurement," said Abhay Thipsay, a retired Bombay High Court judge.
"If a person receives some benefit and consciously chooses to convert for that reason, why should it be considered wrong?"

The law also allows parents, siblings and other relatives to complain to police about an allegedly unlawful conversion, leaving the person accused of causing or assisting it to prove that it was lawful.
Critics say for interfaith couples, that provision adds another potential obstacle to marriages that can already face family opposition.

Indian law allows people of different faiths to marry without converting, but requires a month's notice. Lara Jesani, a lawyer who has helped interfaith couples obtain court protection, said details of planned weddings have sometimes reached relatives and Hindu nationalist groups opposed to them within that notice period.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Critics fear the new law may give families or right-wing organisations a new way to target interfaith couples

blocks.text: Critics fear the new law may give families or right-wing organisations a new way to target interfaith couples
In cases she has handled, she said, families have taken women away, even from the marriage registrar's office.
Now, she fears the new law may give the families or right-wing organisations a new way to target such couples.
"Even when neither intend to convert, [the couples] fear a relative could accuse one partner of trying to convert the other."

The Maharashtra government did not respond to detailed questions from the BBC about these concerns. But when the law was passed, state minister Pankaj Bhoyar said it did not infringe upon the right to change religion. The notification requirement, he said, was intended to establish whether a conversion was voluntary, while allowing the state to act against those brought about by fraud, coercion or inducement.
But Tribhuvan is still worried, an anxiety, he says, which reaches even the small prayer gatherings held closer to home when a church is too far away.
Fifty people might attend, he said, sometimes 100 - and someone who is not Christian might join too.
"If someone else wishes to come and pray, we cannot stop them," he said. "That is what we call the right to choose."
To Thipsay, the retired judge, the precaution points to a larger question.
"If an adult has the power to make major decisions - such as whom to marry - and has been given the right to vote," he said, "why should they not have the power to make this decision too?"

articles.title: Saskatoon man sentenced to house arrest for inciting hatred against Jewish people
articles.summary: Brandon Taylor Moore received an 18-month conditional sentence order, which will be served in the community. He will spend the first six months on house arrest.

image.caption: Brandon Taylor Moore was sentenced to house arrest Monday after pleading guilty earlier this year. (LetsGoBrando45/X.com)

blocks.text: Saskatoon
Brandon Taylor Moore received an 18-month conditional sentence order, which will be served in the community. He will spend the first six months on house arrest.
Advocacy group says sentencing doesn't go far enough
David Katzman says that when he was a teenager in Saskatoon, he believed antisemitism was largely a thing of the past.

He remembers older members of his synagogue, Congregation Agudas Israel, telling him in the 1970s that "antisemitism never truly dies," but "goes to sleep" and waits for the right conditions to return.
"At the time, I thought they were being overly pessimistic. Today, I know they were right," Katzman said in Saskatoon provincial court Monday.
He was giving a victim impact statement at the sentencing for Brandon Taylor Moore, who pleaded guilty earlier this year to publicly inciting hatred against Jewish people.

Moore, 45, was arrested last December after police investigated complaints about antisemitic comments on his account on X, formerly Twitter. He was also charged with wilfully promoting hatred, wilfully promoting antisemitism and unsafe storage of a firearm; those charges were stayed at the conclusion of his sentencing on Monday.

According to the agreed facts on his sentencing, Moore operated an account on X that had approximately 180,000 followers. Between February 2024 and December 2025, Moore communicated "prolifically," with certain statements inciting hatred against Jewish people.
"Those statements included hateful invective directed at Jewish people including public communications calling for their removal or exclusion," Crown prosecutor David Piche said.

As of Monday afternoon, Moore's account was still online, although he hasn't made new posts on it since his arrest in December, when he was released on bail conditions that included not posting anything on the Internet.
Now, as a condition of his sentence, Moore will be required to delete all his posts on it between Feb. 1, 2024, and Dec. 17, 2025.
Katzman, other Jewish people and representatives of Jewish organizations spoke in court of the anxiety, hurt and fear that Moore's posts caused.
Saskatoon man charged with inciting hatred in antisemitic posts online
"Brandon Taylor Moore's posts were not merely offensive or insulting," said Rochelle Direnfeld, on behalf of the Alliance of Canadians Combatting Antisemitism.
"They drew on familiar antisemitic tropes and dehumanizing narratives that have been used for generations to marginalize, expel and persecute Jewish people."
Piche and Moore, who represented himself in court, presented a joint sentencing recommendation for an 18-month conditional sentence order — a jail sentence that is served in the community.
Moore will be under house arrest for the first six months, then have to abide by a curfew of 11 p.m. to 6 a.m. for the following six months.
He must also take personal counselling and educational programming for hate speech as directed, and perform 150 hours of community service.
When Judge Sanjeev Anand asked Moore if he had anything he wanted to say, Moore read a brief prepared statement.
He said that he has served on boards, worked on inner-city outreach, volunteered with Big Brothers Big Sisters of Saskatoon and taught "children's church" at his church for years.
He said that when he watched what was happening to the children in Gaza, "I couldn't look away."
Sentence prompts different reactions
Piche said he thought the sentence struck the right balance between consequences and rehabilitation.

"It shows a person with no record can receive a very significant sentence, going all the way to a CSO right off the bat," he said in a scrum with journalists, adding this was an unusual case for Saskatchewan.
"Hate speech cases are quite rare. So, it was a first for me, and again, prosecutors in our office don't get them very often."
A Jewish advocacy organization said the sentence didn't go far enough.

"We don't believe that the sentence reflects the gravity of the charges or the severity of the harm which Mr. Moore inflicted on the Jewish community," said Richard Robertson, B'nai Brith Canada's director of research and advocacy, who also read a community impact statement into the court's record.
He said B'nai Brith spent years investigating Moore's posts and filed complaints to authorities. Robertson said a plea deal meant not enough evidence was allowed in the sentencing hearing.

"That, in our opinion, was insufficient to really demonstrate the totality of Mr. Moore's antisemitism, the totality of the hate that he incited, and really the veracity of problematic conduct," he said.
The group released a statement saying the sentencing shows provincial governments should establish teams that focus on prosecuting hate crimes.

A United Nations Commission of Inquiry has said that Israel has committed genocide in Gaza, during the war following the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas attack that killed 1,200 people in Israel. The Palestinian death toll from the nearly three-year war has surpassed 74,000, according to Gaza's Health Ministry.

items: Saskatoon man pleads guilty to inciting hatred via antisemitic posts online
Man charged in egging of Saskatoon synagogue wants to make 'reparations' to Jewish community

blocks.text: Moore said that he understood he was in court because of how his words could be read by the public and "that's on me."

Judge Sanjeev Anand told Moore that his comments "crossed a line" by making comments that went beyond a government's actions and were directed toward "an entire people" who have been historically subject to systemic discrimination and attempts at extermination.
"Don't let your passions for individuals who may have been the victims of injustice colour your perspective on the good people who are your neighbours," Anand said.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Hannah Spray works as a reporter and copy editor. She began her journalism career in newspapers, first in her hometown of Meadow Lake, Sask., moving on to Fort St. John, B.C., and then to the Saskatoon StarPhoenix. She joined CBC in 2022. Send story tips confidentially via Signal to HannahSpray.10

articles.title: Journalist to be crowned king in Uganda after bitter succession dispute
articles.summary: Kijanangoma is being crowned amid a dispute over a young heir whom the royal clan does not recognise.

blocks.text: Prince Edward Rukidi Kijanangoma Nyabongo II, who is set to be crowned king of Uganda's Tooro kingdom later, has long been a familiar face in the country.
For many Ugandans, he was known not as the heir to the throne, but as a storyteller, as a long-serving anchor and editor at the state broadcaster.
But Kijanangoma, 56, has now become the subject of media attention himself - his rise to the Tooro throne sparking controversy and widespread reactions beyond the country.

Tooro is one of Uganda's four main officially recognised historical kingdoms. For the last 31 years, it has been headed by King Oyo Nyimba Kabamba Iguru Rukidi IV, who was once known as a "boy king", after ascending to the throne as an infant.
Oyo became king in 1995 at the age of just three, following the death of his father. Then the world's youngest monarch, he ruled until he died last month from cancer, aged just 34.

The coronation is a day for celebration, involving traditional practices starting from midnight. The new king then walks about 4km (2.5 miles) to the official Karuziika royal palace where he is crowned.

A mock fight follows, to signify that kingship does not come easy, and he is then blessed by members of the royal Babiito clan, the Tooro kingdom's Information Minister Charles Mwanguhya told the BBC Focus on Africa podcast.

He performs other ceremonies that signifies his assumption of the throne, before he sits on the throne and an actual crown placed on his head to signify his new authority, his new position as the new Tooro king.
But the selection of Kijanangoma as king was far from straightforward.

According to tradition, a recognised son of the late king should succeed him. Close members of the royal family said Oyo had left a young son and a will with instructions that the child should be next on the throne.
But the son has never been revealed to the public and nor was he recognised by the committee of 21 Babiito clan members who choose the king and eventually selected Kijanangoma.
The late King Oyo was never publicly married, and little is known about his wife or their son.
Nonetheless his mother, Queen Best Kemigisa, argued that the late king's will ought to have been respected.
However, the royal succession committee ignored her wishes, insisting their selection process was conducted in accordance with Tooro customs and traditions.
The new king has thus found himself at the centre of a succession dispute, with Kemigisa and her close relatives unhappy with the outcome.
Kemigisa referred to Kijanangoma's selection as the "announcement of a second king" being "made after the will of King Oyo was read to members of the royal family".
"As a mother, that was extraordinarily painful," she said, describing celebrations for the next king taking place "only metres from where my son's body lay".
The queen later said Oyo's son, who was in the US state of Texas, had been due to return home but that could not happen amid a "tense and polarised succession dispute".
"No child should be placed in circumstances where returning to his father's homeland could mean being drawn into hostility and conflict," Kemigisa asserted in a post on X.

But according to the Tooro kingdom's information minister, the son being talked about "hasn't been presented anywhere, which means there is a growing acceptance that sad as it may be, King Oyo didn't leave a son behind".
While King Oyo inherited the crown from his father, Mwanguhya told the BBC "the crown has moved to a different line within the ruling clan".
A king must come from the Babiito clan, specifically the lineage of King George David Matthew Kamurasi Rukidi III, according to royal palace sources.
Kijanangoma and the late King Oyo are cousins. Both are grandsons of Rukidi III, the 11th king, or Omukama, who ruled the Tooro kingdom from 1928 to 1965.
Kijanangoma was among several people who were considered for the role, including Prince George Desmond Kamurasi, who plays football for one of the UK's best-known amateur clubs.
According to the succession committee, the South East Dons captain and goalkeeper declined the offer of the throne, citing other responsibilities.
After he was formally announced, Kijanangoma promised that the palace would be open to the people, while vowing to focus on unity and development.
"I ask you for one thing - they have given me this title as king but I cannot work alone, I have to work with you," he said.
Uganda's traditional kings have no formal political authority, but they retain cultural influence and command significant loyalty in the communities they lead.
The country is home to four main kingdoms, the largest and most prominent being Buganda in the central region, which encompasses the capital Kampala.
The kingdoms were abolished in 1967, but the government under President Yoweri Museveni restored them in the early 1990s.
The government said this was to promote cultural pride and national unity, but the move has also been interpreted as a way of appeasing communities and fostering political loyalty.

Amid the succession dispute, the government backed the Babiito clan's choice of Kijanangoma. Attorney General Sam Mayanja said the Tooro kingdom was cleared to go ahead with the coronation, as there had not been a formal complaint against him.
The date of the coronation was announced by the government and Museveni is scheduled to attend.
The president's son and the head of the military, Muhoozi Kainerugaba, has also publicly supported Kijanangoma. "Long may he reign," he posted on X.
Kijanangoma's very name points to his royal heritage.
His father, the first Kijanangoma, was born in the year King Rukidi III became king. The king gave him the name, which means the "one who comes with the royal drum".
The drum of royalty, foretold two generations earlier, is now returning to its bearer.
Kijanangoma was born in 1970 and raised at their family home at Kidukuru village in Fort Portal, about 300 km (186 miles) from Kampala.
He left the village to pursue further studies and graduated with a mass communication degree from Uganda's prestigious Makerere University in 1999.
He worked as a broadcaster in a career spanning more than two decades, including in neighbouring Rwanda and at home, with the Uganda Broadcasting Corporation.

The years spent engaging with the public, the interactions with leaders and the exposure to national affairs in his work as a journalist may yet serve him well as he returns to the community he came from, this time as their leader.
After he was named king, Kijanangoma said he would use the connections he had built up over 21 years working as a journalist "to get good things for our people".
His mother, Assimwe Yusta Kijanangoma, is confident that he is well prepared for his new role. She says his upbringing was deeply rooted in tradition.
"I really raised him with the teachings of the old kingdom of a cane and instructions and scolding. I laugh with him, and other times I scold him," she told the BBC.
She added: "Eddy is well-mannered, he does not fight, or shout, even when wronged, he says a few words and does not go so much into it."
She feels good for her son, although she admits to having mixed emotions, especially as her son is taking over after the death of a "great man".

articles.title: Election lawyer seeks TRO vs law moving barangay, SK polls to 2028
articles.summary: He asks the Supreme Court to strike down the law moving the polls to 2028.

blocks.text: September 29, 2026 | 7:30am
MANILA, Philippines — Election lawyer Romulo Macalintal asked the Supreme Court to strike down the law postponing the November 2026 Barangay and Sangguniang Kabataan Elections to November 2028.

Macalintal filed a petition for certiorari and prohibition on Monday, September 28 challenging the constitutionality of Republic Act 12326, naming the Office of the President, Senate, House of Representatives and Commission on Elections as respondents.
He also sought an immediate status quo ante order, temporary restraining order and writ of preliminary injunction to halt the law's implementation.
"I thought 'forever' was only in love. Turns out 'forever' also exists in barangay election postponements," Macalintal told reporters in Filipino at the Supreme Court grounds.
"That is why we will fight this, because this postponement is far too long. And our right to vote was taken away from us by our lawmakers," he added.
'Whimsical' 3-year delay
Macalintal argued that the law infringes on the electorate's right of suffrage under the guise of "fixing" the term of barangay officials at five years.
The last BSKE was held on Oct. 30, 2023, while the next elections were originally scheduled for December 2025.
Congress later moved the polls to November 2026 through Republic Act 12232, which also adjusted the term of office to four years.
Republic Act 12326, meanwhile, postpones the elections by another two years to November 2028, resulting in a cumulative three-year delay from the original December 2025 schedule.
Macalintal argued that the repeated deferrals deprives voters of their right to vote for an unreasonably long period.

The delay, he said, is a "very clear grave abuse of discretion amounting to lack or excess of jurisdiction on the part of Congress." He also called the postponement "very apparent arbitrary and whimsical," citing Macalintal v. Senate and Macalintal v. COMELEC.
'Lightning speed'
Macalintal also questioned how quickly the law was enacted.
President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. signed Republic Act 12326 on September 24, with the law taking effect immediately upon its publication the following day.

"It was practically enacted at lightning speed, mabilis pa sa kidlat, or in apparent haste, and with the clear and direct effect of shutting the courthouse doors to Petitioner and similarly situated citizens, leaving them with a dangerously narrow window to study, research, and draft a well-founded petition, considering that the November 2, 2026 BSKE is barely one month and a few days away," Macalintal said.
He also challenged the administration's justifications for postponement, including the use of incumbent officials to help fight crime, manage floods and coordinate garbage disposal.

Macalintal argued that these are routine administrative functions that do not meet what he described as the strict constitutional standards for postponing elections established in Macalintal v. Comelec.
He also questioned justifications raised during congressional deliberations involving funding risks from the global oil crisis and conflicts in the Middle East.
Macalintal pointed out that those external crises did not prevent the government from holding the Sept. 14, 2026 elections in the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao.
He also cited the Comelec's declaration that it was fully prepared for the November 2026 BSKE, arguing that postponement would waste billions of pesos already spent on preparations.
Holdover provision challenged
Beyond the postponement itself, Macalintal also challenged the law's transitory provision, which treats the holdover period of incumbent officials as a completed term.

He argued that the provision conflates "term of office" with "tenure of office" and effectively amounts to the legislative appointment of holdover officials, contrary to the constitutional requirement that barangay officials be elected.
The law, he said, effectively creates a "two-year term extension" without clearly identifying the provision that grants it.

articles.title: In-laws arrested on suspicion of murder after New York Times engineer shot dead in California
articles.summary:
Police arrest couple in their 70s after Jonathan McKinsey, 40, found dead in park in Bay Area city of Dublin

A married couple in their 70s have been arrested for allegedly shooting and…

blocks.text: A married couple in their 70s have been arrested for allegedly shooting and killing their son-in-law, a New York Times engineer, in broad daylight at a suburban Bay Area park.

A police officer found Jonathan McKinsey, 40, lying on the ground with multiple gunshot wounds in a park in Dublin, California, a small city about 35 miles east of San Francisco. Around the time the officer discovered him, 911 calls began pouring in from witnesses reporting the shooting.
McKinsey was pronounced dead at the scene, according to a press release from the city of Dublin on Sunday.
He had been the head of engineering for the New York Times’s games department for nearly four years, according to his LinkedIn page.

Witnesses told police that the suspected shooters, identified as Shouyong Zhang and Shili Chen, both 77, were still in the area. The pair, identified by police as McKinsey’s in-laws, were arrested on suspicion of murder shortly after the shooting.
Witnesses also told CBS News that the suspects were both wearing masks, and each took a turn shooting the victim.
An arraignment is scheduled for Wednesday, the San Francisco Chronicle reported. Police have not indicated a motive for the shooting.
Court records cited in local media reports show McKinsey and his wife had been engaged in a legal battle over child custody and allegations of domestic and child abuse.

The city of Dublin has had one homicide per year between 2023 and 2025, while the number of reported domestic violence incidents increased from 121 in 2024 to 131 in 2025, according to the city’s crime data.

articles.title: Calgary-Edmonton high-speed rail project moves forward with new commitments from Alberta, feds
articles.summary: Plans for high-speed rail service between Calgary, Red Deer and Edmonton are moving forward with new commitments from the governments of Alberta and Canada. The province says it is preparing to…

image.caption: The Alberta government says it is preparing to launch a formal process for private-sector proponents to submit proposals for a high-speed rail project between Calgary, Red Deer and Edmonton. Premier Danielle Smith and provincial Transportation Minister Devin Dreeshen are pictured during an earlier p

blocks.text: Calgary·New

Plans for high-speed rail service between Calgary, Red Deer and Edmonton are moving forward with new commitments from the governments of Alberta and Canada. The province says it is preparing to launch a formal process for private-sector proponents of the rail project to submit proposals, and the federal government has committed to referring the project to Ottawa's Major Projects Office.
Proposed rail service would get passengers from one city to the other through Red Deer in under 2 hours
Plans for high-speed rail service between Calgary and Edmonton are moving forward with new commitments from the governments of Alberta and Canada, the province announced Monday.
The province says it is preparing to launch a formal process for private-sector proponents of the rail project to submit proposals.

"Throughout the development of Alberta’s Passenger Rail Master Plan, we heard that a high-speed passenger rail connection between Calgary and Edmonton via Red Deer is a priority for Albertans," provincial Transportation Minister Devin Dreeshen said.

Through that plan, the province found that high-speed rail service between Edmonton and Calgary through Red Deer with more than one train an hour was a "feasible" project "that could generate the greatest benefits for Alberta over 30 years."

The plan, which included a rail network more than 500 kilometres long that also includes service between Calgary and Banff and all-day service to and from the Calgary and Edmonton airports, also came with a $15-million investment over the next three years.
"We are excited to move forward with this project, which will transform the way Albertans travel," Dreeshen said.
High-speed passenger rail service is now a goal in Alberta

After the formal request for proposals is launched, the province plans to select a private-sector proponent for the project by April 2027, with minimal financial investment expected from the provincial government.

With the area between Calgary, Edmonton and Red Deer home to about 80 per cent of Alberta's population, Premier Danielle Smith said connecting the three cities with high-speed rail service "would be a generational investment in Alberta’s future."
"As our province continues to grow, we need to build the infrastructure that keeps people, businesses and our economy moving," she said.

items: Alberta government eyes downtown-to-airport trains as 1st key project of passenger rail plan
'Timing is now' as Canmore pushes for stop in potential Calgary-Banff rail service

blocks.text: The province expects the proposed high-speed rail connection, going at speeds of up to 320 km/h on new rail tracks in a dedicated corridor, would get passengers between downtown Edmonton and downtown Calgary in one hour and 45 minutes.

"By working with the federal government, we are taking the next steps toward a project that could strengthen one of Canada’s fastest-growing economic corridors and support Alberta’s growth for decades to come," Smith said.
The province's announcement on Monday also came with a commitment from the Government of Canada that the project corridor will be referred to the federal Major Projects Office.
The federal government says Ottawa would work with Alberta to advance the project once the province has selected a private proponent.

“High-speed rail has great potential to reshape the way people move in Canada, and supports Alberta's economic growth, productivity and regional connectivity," said Steven MacKinnon, the federal minister of transport.
"Today's collaboration demonstrates our shared commitment to exploring opportunities that could deliver lasting benefits for Albertans and Canadians."

Amir Said is a multimedia journalist with CBC Calgary. He is an alumnus of the University of Regina, and his award-winning work as a writer and photographer has been published by outlets across Canada, including Postmedia, The Hill Times and The Narwhal. articles.title: Tennessee to execute a woman for first time in 200 years after governor denies clemency
articles.summary:
Lawyers for Christa Pike, 50, convicted of killing classmate in Knoxville in 1995, ask supreme court to grant stay

Christa Pike was 18 when she killed a classmate in a jealous rage and…

blocks.text: Christa Pike was 18 when she killed a classmate in a jealous rage and became one of the youngest women to be sent to death row. Now 50, she is scheduled to be put to death on Wednesday in what would be Tennessee’s first execution of a woman in 200 years.

Pike and her boyfriend were convicted in the 1995 killing of 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer, their classmate at Knoxville Job Corps. Prosecutors said Pike feared Slemmer was a romantic rival and lured her to a secluded area where she and her boyfriend tortured and killed Slemmer.
The case received widespread attention because of the brutality of the killing, the ages of the people involved, and because a satanic symbol was carved into the victim’s body.

Pike does not deny her guilt, but her attorneys and supporters argue a death sentence is not appropriate for a crime committed at that age by a teen with untreated mental illness after a childhood of brutal sexual abuse and neglect. Slemmer’s mother wants the lethal injection go forward, saying she has waited decades to see Pike’s sentence carried out.
Tennessee governor Bill Lee announced Monday that he would not grant clemency. Pike’s attorneys have asked the supreme court to stay the execution.
Pike’s attorneys said she experienced an exceptionally traumatic and abusive childhood.

Assistant federal defender Stephen Ferrell said Pike was sexually abused starting from when she was a toddler and that she was raped at 11 and 17. He said Pike’s lawyers at the penalty phase of her trial did not present the jury with what he said was critical information about her past or argue that her age should be a consideration.

Pike was later diagnosed with bipolar disorder and post-traumatic stress disorder. Pike told police she initially only wanted to fight Slemmer but ended up killing her in a frenzied attack. In her clemency petition, Pike’s attorneys said her untreated mental illness and background made her unable to “put the brakes on”.

“I was a mentally ill 18-year-old kid. It took me numerous years to even realize the gravity of what I’d done. Even more to accept how many lives I affected. I took the life of someone’s child, sister, friend. It sickens me now to think I had the ability to commit such a crime,” Pike said in a statement included in her clemency petition.

Ferrell said more today is known about adolescent brain development and that Pike’s death sentence is an outlier. He noted that Pike’s boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, who was 17 at the time, was sentenced to life with the possibility of parole because of his age. He was denied parole last year. A third teen admitted to being an accessory and received probation.
Speaking by telephone from Florida, Slemmer’s mother, May Martinez, said her daughter volunteered with the Special Olympics, loved roller skating and wanted to pursue a career in computers.
“She was easygoing. She was a computer geek to begin with. She and my husband would build and tear apart the computers constantly,” Martinez said. “She trusted everybody, and that was her downfall.”

The killing rocked the city of Knoxville. Prosecutors said Pike cut Slemmer with a box-cutter and beat her with a large chunk of asphalt. Elements of the crime stoked fears of Satan worship during the “satanic panic” of the 1980s and 1990s. Shipp, Pike’s boyfriend, has admitted that he was the one who carved a pentagram, a star-shaped symbol associated with Satanism, into her body.
If Pike’s execution proceeds as scheduled, it would be Tennessee’s first execution of a woman since 1820, Maher said.
Executions of female inmates are also rare in the US. Since 1976, 18 women have been executed in the country, representing about 1% of all executions, according to the center.
Most recently, Missouri in 2023 executed Amber McLaughlin, a transgender woman, for a 2003 killing, in what is believed to be the first execution of a transgender woman in the US.
In 2021, the federal government executed Lisa Montgomery, marking the first time in nearly seven decades that the US government has put a female inmate to death. Georgia executed a woman in 2015.

articles.title: Melbourne human rights activist disappears in Cambodia as wife urges Albanese government help
articles.summary:
Tran Hiep, a 50-year-old Australian Vietnamese anti-human trafficking campaigner, not heard from since 18 September

The wife of an Australian activist missing in Cambodia has implored the…

blocks.text: The wife of an Australian activist missing in Cambodia has implored the federal government to find him and bring him home.

Tran Hiep, a 50-year-old Australian Vietnamese democracy campaigner, was due to return to Bangkok, Thailand, to reunite with his wife Chloe Dang after a short trip to Phnom Penh, Cambodia, to meet with human rights defenders.
But he never boarded his flight and has not communicated with his wife since 18 September, leaving her worried for his safety.
“My family and I are really worried about his safety, and we just only want to know where he is and what happened to him,” Dang said from Bangkok airport before boarding a flight to Melbourne.
“My husband deserves protection, and I really hope the Australian government will continue to put pressure on Cambodia to do an investigation to find out where he is right now.”

Hiep, a freelance IT professional who founded the Australian Alliance to Combat Human Trafficking, was travelling with another human rights activist Nguyen Duc Thuan, who is also Vietnamese and holds a Norwegian passport.
The pair travelled to Cambodia to meet with dissident Vietnamese activists for training.

blocks.caption: Tran Hiep has not communicated with his wife since 18 September

blocks.text: Vietnam in recent years has ramped up its crackdown on dissidents, with more than 55 activists arrested under broad criminal laws in 2025.
Civil society groups and United Nations human rights experts have repeatedly warned of growing co-operation between Vietnamese authorities and neighbouring governments targeting advocates.

Viet Tan, a pro-democracy diaspora political party, has described the pair’s disappearance as concerning given previous cases involving Vietnamese dissidents vanishing in neighbouring countries and subsequently appearing in custody in Vietnam.
“Their disappearance is not an ordinary ‘missing person’ incident. Both men are long-time human rights advocates and Viet Tan members,” the organisation said.
Dang, 36, said fretting over her husband’s whereabouts had taken a psychological toll.
“It’s been 11 days and I’m really in the dark,” she said, choking back tears.
“I don’t know where he is and how he’s doing – it’s driving me crazy.
“Everything is really uncertain.”
The Australian government confirmed consular officials were in contact with Dang but declined to comment further.
“The Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade is providing consular assistance to the family of an Australian reported missing in Cambodia,” a department spokesperson said on Monday.
The families of the missing men have filed an appeal with the UN working group on enforced or involuntary disappearances.
